high_financial_impact.title: Auto-Refill Dispensing Without a Beneficiary Request
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Section 200 expressly prohibits automatic delivery and predetermined refill schedules without a specific beneficiary or caregiver request, and distinguishes a refill request from a prescription renewal. The rule is operationally difficult to observe because claims contain dispensing dates and quantities but not necessarily the request event.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: Its business model is directly tied to refill cadence, with high volume-growth objectives and willingness to exploit ambiguity.

archetypes.name: Enteral/parenteral nutrition supplier
archetypes.why: Recurring nutrition supplies and monthly therapy periods create repeated opportunities to ship without contemporaneous beneficiary confirmation.

archetypes.name: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: Outsourced beneficiary acquisition and high coordination risk make scripted refill outreach and weak request controls plausible.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: High beneficiary reach and remote operations can scale automated refill programs while limiting direct beneficiary interaction.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Increasing recurring-supply volume, reducing cancellation and lapse rates, and converting prescription renewals into billable shipments without a separate beneficiary request.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Claims arrive at highly regular intervals, often near the maximum allowable quantity or before expected depletion, despite no documented contact. Shipments continue after death, hospice enrollment, institutional admission, therapy discontinuation, or a change in equipment. A physician renewal precedes shipment but no beneficiary request is recorded.
detection_signals: Calculate refill interval variance and flag near-deterministic shipment schedules over six or more cycles.
Flag refills with no documented beneficiary/caregiver request within the required pre-dispensing window.
Flag shipments after death, hospice election, institutional admission, therapy discontinuation, or equipment return.
Compare billed quantity and days' supply with prior utilization, remaining inventory, and early-refill history.
Measure beneficiary complaint, return-to-supplier, unopened-package, and reversal rates by supplier and marketer.
graph_signals: Link beneficiaries to common call centers, marketers, scripts, phone numbers, email domains, or shipping addresses.
Identify ordering providers or marketers associated with unusually high refill rates and low documented request rates.
Detect common shipment destinations, representative payees, or caregiver contacts across unrelated beneficiaries.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Beneficiaries or caregivers may make standing or recurring requests, and some clinical situations require regular supplies. Caregiver documentation may be stored outside the claim system or represented by a portal interaction rather than a call.
disambiguating_evidence: Obtain dated call recordings, portal logs, SMS confirmations, refill forms, caregiver authorization, and shipment acknowledgments.
Verify the beneficiary had the underlying DME and ongoing medical necessity at each refill.
Review returned or unopened supplies, inventory, and delivery confirmation.
Separate prescription renewal documentation from the required beneficiary or caregiver refill request.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT r.* FROM refill_claims r WHERE r.paid_amount>0 AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM refill_requests q WHERE q.beneficiary_id=r.beneficiary_id AND q.supplier_npi=r.supplier_npi AND q.request_time <= r.dispense_time AND q.request_time > r.dispense_time-INTERVAL '90 day') OR r.dispense_date IN (SELECT event_date FROM beneficiary_status_events WHERE event_type IN ('DEATH','HOSPICE','INSTITUTIONAL_STAY','EQUIPMENT_RETURN'));

explicit: 200 - Automatic Mailing/Delivery of DMEPOS
cms_source.inference: The prohibition is explicit; the claim-based indicators are proxies for the otherwise non-claim refill-request event.

high_financial_impact.title: Lead-Generated Refill-and-Order Network
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Section 200 requires a specific beneficiary or caregiver request before repetitive supplies are dispensed, while sections 10.2 and 110.4 permit recurring supply billing when the beneficiary has the underlying DME and medical necessity continues. A lead-generation or telehealth network can create apparently valid orders across many suppliers while the actual refill-request process is weak, standardized, or supplier-initiated.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Access to beneficiaries 5, referral relationships 5, geographic reach 5, and volume-growth objective 5 support centralized remote order generation at scale; compliance sophistication 2 increases refill-control risk.

archetypes.name: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: Access to beneficiaries 5, referral relationships 5, coordination with others 5, and willingness to exploit ambiguity 4 make outsourced beneficiary acquisition and weak control over refill requests plausible.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: Volume-growth objective 5 and referral relationships 4 can create pressure to accept high-volume leads before beneficiary-request controls mature; compliance sophistication is only 2.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: The business model monetizes refill cadence directly, with recurring-supply and frequency rules creating a strong incentive to convert lead-generated contacts into repeated claims.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5, access to beneficiaries 5, risk tolerance 5, and willingness to exploit ambiguity 5 support coordinated creation of orders, refill attestations, and beneficiary participation across entities.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Recurring monthly or periodic supply revenue, increased beneficiary lifetime value, and conversion of a single remotely generated order into repeated claims without equivalent clinical or fulfillment effort.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: High volumes of recurring supply HCPCS codes linked to common ordering providers, marketer-associated beneficiary cohorts, or multiple supplier NPIs; refill claims occur at highly regular intervals, often near maximum allowable quantities or frequency limits. Claims may show the same supply category across numerous beneficiaries with little variation, despite different diagnoses, geography, or care settings.
detection_signals: For each supplier, calculate the percentage of refill claims preceded by a documented beneficiary/caregiver request within a defined operational window; flag rates below the plan benchmark.

Calculate ordering-provider and marketer-linked beneficiary concentration using Herfindahl-Hirschman Index; flag suppliers where the top 5 ordering providers account for more than 50% of recurring-supply beneficiaries or where one provider is shared across multiple suppliers.
Flag refill intervals with coefficient of variation below 0.10 across at least four cycles when beneficiary-request timestamps are absent or identical across many beneficiaries.
Flag beneficiaries receiving the same supply category from multiple network suppliers within the same expected replacement interval.
Compare billed units with prior utilization, documented DME ownership, and days since last shipment; flag repeated claims at or near frequency limits.
graph_signals: Bipartite graph showing one lead-generation entity or call-center-associated address connected to many beneficiaries, ordering providers, and supplier NPIs.
Community detection identifying supplier-ordering-provider-beneficiary clusters with unusually high internal connectivity and low external referral diversity.
Shared telephone numbers, beneficiary-contact addresses, domains, bank accounts, or ownership links among supposedly independent suppliers receiving the same lead cohorts.
Ordering providers whose recurring-supply beneficiaries are disproportionately concentrated among suppliers using the same marketer or fulfillment vendor.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Legitimate mail-order suppliers may have standardized refill cycles, centralized call centers, and common ordering providers serving medically homogeneous populations. Beneficiaries with chronic conditions may appropriately receive the same quantities at regular intervals.
disambiguating_evidence: Beneficiary-initiated request recordings, portal logs, call metadata, or authenticated refill confirmations tied to each shipment.
Shipment tracking, delivery confirmation, return records, and evidence that the beneficiary possessed and continued to use the underlying DME.
Clinical records supporting continuing medical necessity and quantities, including evidence that supplies were not stockpiled.
Contracts, compensation arrangements, and compliance oversight involving lead generators and ordering providers.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: WITH refill AS (SELECT supplier_npi, beneficiary_id, ordering_npi, hcpcs, service_date, units, request_timestamp, shipment_tracking_id FROM dme_claims WHERE claim_type = 'recurring_supply') SELECT supplier_npi, COUNT(*) AS claims, AVG(CASE WHEN request_timestamp IS NULL THEN 1.0 ELSE 0.0 END) AS no_request_rate, COUNT(DISTINCT ordering_npi) AS ordering_count, COUNT(DISTINCT beneficiary_id) AS beneficiary_count FROM refill GROUP BY supplier_npi HAVING no_request_rate > 0.20 OR COUNT(*) >= 1000 AND COUNT(DISTINCT ordering_npi) <= 5;

explicit: Section 200 - Automatic Mailing/Delivery of DMEPOS
Section 10.2 - Coverage Table for DME Claims
Section 110.4 - Frequency of Claims for Repetitive Services
cms_source.inference: The corpus expressly prohibits supplier-initiated automatic refills. The network and lead-generation mechanism, and the use of graph concentration as evidence, are analytic inferences.

high_financial_impact.title: Distributed Ordering-Provider Concentration and Medical-Necessity Manufacture
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 10.1.2, 10.1.3, 30.3, 100.1, 100.2, and 100.2.2 require physician or authorized-practitioner orders and supporting medical-necessity documentation, but permit clinician employees to prepare portions of documentation subject to physician review. A network can make each individual supplier appear ordinary while a small set of clinicians generate a disproportionate volume of orders with templated or product-specific medical-necessity narratives.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Beneficiary access 5, referral relationships 5, and geographic reach 5 support centralized remote ordering, while compliance sophistication 2 creates risk that clinician independence and documentation quality are not validated.

archetypes.name: Physician practice dispensing or ordering DME
archetypes.why: Access to beneficiaries 5 and referral relationships 5 create direct control over both the order and supporting narrative, producing a strong self-referral and documentation-shaping risk.

archetypes.name: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and referral relationships 5 make it plausible for marketers to steer beneficiaries toward a concentrated ordering-provider panel.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5, risk tolerance 5, and access to beneficiaries 5 support deliberate clinician-supplier-beneficiary coordination.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Generating more orders for high-margin or recurring DMEPOS products, increasing beneficiary conversion, and reducing order-acquisition costs through a small repeat-referral clinician panel.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: A limited number of ordering providers account for a large share of a supplier's beneficiaries or a specific HCPCS family. Diagnoses, order text, estimated length of need, and accessory combinations are highly standardized. Ordering-provider concentration persists across multiple supplier NPIs, states, or marketers, and claims surge after a new lead source is activated.
detection_signals: Calculate ordering-provider concentration by supplier, HCPCS family, diagnosis, and month; flag top-provider share above 40% or HHI above peer percentile.
Measure template similarity of order narratives, CMNs, or supporting notes; flag high textual similarity across unrelated beneficiaries.
Flag ordering providers whose DMEPOS order volume is extreme relative to their Medicare patient panel, specialty, or evaluation-and-management activity.
Flag short intervals between beneficiary enrollment, telehealth encounter, order signature, and high-volume DMEPOS claim across many beneficiaries.
Compare order diagnoses and equipment combinations with clinical encounters, functional findings, and prior equipment history; flag product-specific diagnosis patterns.
graph_signals: One ordering provider connected to many suppliers, marketers, and beneficiaries, especially across multiple states.
Shared ordering-provider panels between suppliers using the same marketer, call center, address, or bank account.
Bipartite communities where a clinician orders nearly identical HCPCS combinations for beneficiaries acquired by the same lead source.
Ordering providers with unusually high centrality in the network despite limited independent clinical activity.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Specialists may legitimately order a narrow range of equipment for a concentrated disease population. Large telehealth practices may use standardized templates, and authorized employees may prepare documentation for physician review.
disambiguating_evidence: Complete clinical records, encounter notes, functional assessments, and evidence of physician review and independent clinical judgment.
Signature provenance, timestamps, electronic-authentication logs, and identification of the person completing documentation.
Referral, marketing, ownership, and compensation records between clinicians, suppliers, and lead generators.
Beneficiary interviews confirming the encounter, symptoms, order, and receipt of equipment.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT ordering_npi, COUNT(DISTINCT beneficiary_id) AS beneficiaries, COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_npi) AS suppliers, COUNT(*) AS claims, COUNT(DISTINCT diagnosis_hcpcs_signature) AS signatures FROM dme_claims GROUP BY ordering_npi HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT beneficiary_id) > 500 AND COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_npi) >= 3 AND COUNT(DISTINCT diagnosis_hcpcs_signature) <= 10;

Section 10.1.3 - Prosthetics and Orthotics - Coverage Definition
Section 100.1 - Written Order Prior to Delivery
Section 100.2.1 - Completion of Certificate of Medical Necessity Forms
Section 100.2.2 - Evidence of Medical Necessity for PEN Therapy

high_financial_impact.title: Oxygen Ownership and Modifier Stack
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Oxygen payment changes based on whether stationary and portable systems are rented or owned, while QG/QF/QB modifiers alter payment and prohibit certain additive combinations. Incorrect or strategically inconsistent ownership, flow-rate, or modifier data can move a beneficiary between materially different payment paths.

archetypes.name: Oxygen/respiratory equipment supplier
archetypes.why: The business model is monthly and date-driven, with direct operational control over equipment ownership status and prescribed flow-rate data.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: Technical coding sophistication (5) and willingness to exploit ambiguity (5) support deliberate modifier and ownership-path optimization.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: High volume-growth objective (5) and referral relationships (4) create incentives to standardize high-paying oxygen configurations across a large beneficiary base.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: Coordination with HHAs (4) and access to clinical observations can affect whether oxygen is characterized as rented, owned, stationary, or portable.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: The payment differential between ordinary stationary oxygen, high-flow QG/QB treatment, portable add-ons, and contents fees can be substantial over recurring monthly claims. Misstating ownership or stacking prohibited add-ons can increase payment.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: QG or QB claims with portable add-ons inconsistent with the oxygen billing chart; QF or QB lines accompanied by separately paid portable monthly equipment; changes from rented to owned status without a purchase claim; oxygen contents fees billed when equipment is rented or absent; flow-rate modifiers inconsistent with the order or testing.
detection_signals: Rate of QG, QF, QB, or high-flow claims by supplier compared with regional peers.
Beneficiary-months with mutually exclusive stationary, portable, and contents payments.
Ownership-status transitions without a corresponding purchase, title, or equipment history event.
Portable oxygen claims within 30 days before or after QG claims despite the stated CWF edit.
Average prescribed flow rates just above modifier thresholds, such as greater than 4 LPM, by ordering provider.
graph_signals: Ordering providers with unusually concentrated high-flow or QB/QF oxygen referrals.
Supplier-beneficiary clusters receiving identical flow-rate patterns or modifier combinations.
Shared respiratory therapists, call centers, addresses, or ownership among suppliers billing the same beneficiaries.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Clinical needs can change, and a patient may legitimately use different stationary and portable systems. Ownership can change after a rental cap or supplier transfer. Claims history may also be incomplete across contractors or during transitions.
disambiguating_evidence: Current oxygen order, testing results, flow rates at rest and during activity, and equipment inventory.
Title, rental, purchase, and supplier-transfer records.
Delivery and usage documentation for portable and stationary systems.
Cross-MAC claims history and remittance records for the 30-day oxygen edit.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS oxygen_months, SUM(paid_amount) AS paid FROM oxygen_claims o WHERE (o.modifier IN ('QG','QF','QB') OR o.hcpcs IN (portable_oxygen_codes, contents_codes)) AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM oxygen_claims x WHERE x.beneficiary_id=o.beneficiary_id AND x.service_date BETWEEN o.service_date-30 AND o.service_date+30 AND mutually_exclusive(o,x)=1) GROUP BY supplier_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 OR AVG(CASE WHEN prescribed_flow_lpm > 4 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) > 0.30;

explicit: 30.6 - Oxygen and Oxygen Equipment
30.6.1 - Adjustments to Monthly Oxygen Fee
130.6 - Billing for Oxygen and Oxygen Equipment
130.6.1 - Oxygen Equipment and Contents Billing Chart
cms_source.inference: The payment combinations and modifier rules are explicit; the fraud-risk interpretation is that inconsistent ownership, flow, or modifier data could be used to select a higher-paying path.

high_financial_impact.title: Capped-Rental Episode Reset Across Suppliers
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: A supplier change does not restart a capped-rental episode, and an interruption exceeding the permitted period requires new prescription and medical-necessity documentation. Separately, an overlapping inpatient or SNF stay can reset the anniversary date when it overlaps the anniversary date but does not span the entire month. These valid exceptions can be misapplied to create duplicate or extended rental periods.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Maximum coordination (5), risk tolerance (5), Medicare dependence (5), and volume objective (5) support distributed manipulation of supplier transitions and rental histories.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: The business model depends on recurring cadence, with volume objective (4) and ambiguity tolerance (4).

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: Growth objective (5), coordination (3), and audit awareness (2) make episode tracking vulnerable during rapid beneficiary and supplier expansion.

archetypes.name: Multi-state supplier
archetypes.why: Geographic reach (5) can fragment episode history across contractors, states, or NPIs.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Restarting or extending the rental sequence can generate additional monthly rental payments beyond the beneficiary's existing 15-month episode and may shift maintenance obligations between suppliers.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: New supplier claims use KH or an apparent first-month indicator after prior paid rental months; overlapping suppliers bill the same or similar HCPCS; claims resume after a short interruption without required new documentation; anniversary dates shift without a matching inpatient or SNF overlap; rental continues beyond 15 counted months.
detection_signals: Beneficiary-equipment episodes with more than 15 paid rental months absent a validated reset.
Number of supplier changes during a single equipment episode.
New KH claims within 12 months of a prior supplier's KJ or month-10/15 claim.
Rental claims with gaps shorter than 60 days but new prescriptions or apparent new episodes.
Anniversary-date changes not supported by an inpatient or SNF stay overlapping the original anniversary date.
graph_signals: Sequential supplier transfers involving shared ownership, bank accounts, addresses, phone numbers, or billing personnel.
Supplier-ordering-provider pairs recurring across the same beneficiaries at episode boundaries.
Beneficiary clusters transferred among several related NPIs shortly before rental caps.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Supplier changes, hospitalization, equipment loss, and genuine changes in medical need can produce legitimate episode adjustments. Claims histories may also be incomplete when beneficiaries move between managed care and FFS.
disambiguating_evidence: Complete cross-MAC and Medicare Advantage equipment history.
Inpatient/SNF admission, discharge, and anniversary-date records.
New prescription, proof that prior medical necessity ended, and supplier statement for a true post-break episode.
Equipment serial numbers, delivery records, and title or maintenance responsibility.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: WITH episodes AS (SELECT beneficiary_id, normalized_equipment_group, COUNT(DISTINCT rental_month) paid_months, MIN(service_date) first_date, MAX(service_date) last_date, COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_id) suppliers FROM capped_rental_claims GROUP BY beneficiary_id, normalized_equipment_group) SELECT * FROM episodes WHERE paid_months > 15 OR suppliers >= 3 OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM capped_rental_claims c WHERE c.is_first_month=1 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM capped_rental_claims p WHERE p.beneficiary_id=c.beneficiary_id AND p.normalized_equipment_group=c.normalized_equipment_group AND p.service_date < c.service_date AND p.paid_months > 3));

210 - CWF Crossover Editing for DMEPOS Claims During an Inpatient Stay
211.2 - Partial Month Stays for Capped Rental Equipment
10.3 - Beneficiaries Previously Enrolled in Managed Care Who Return to Traditional FFS

high_financial_impact.title: Rotating Supplier Network Around Capped-Rental Episodes
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 30.5.4, 110.4, and 211.2 require rental continuity across supplier changes and preserve the original or properly reset anniversary date. A coordinated network may create fragmented billing across supplier NPIs, exploiting weak longitudinal linkage to make one continuous episode appear to be multiple starts or to obscure responsibility after the fifteenth month.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5, risk tolerance 5, Medicare dependence 5, and geographic reach 4 support deliberate supplier rotation and beneficiary-level episode manipulation.

archetypes.name: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and beneficiary access 5 make it plausible for leads and equipment to be transferred among related suppliers, while compliance sophistication 2 creates continuity-control weaknesses.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: Growth objective 5 and coordination 3 can produce rapid NPI or branch expansion in which rental history is not integrated, creating opportunities for duplicate starts even without a fully organized ring.

archetypes.name: Supplier with unusually high Medicare concentration
archetypes.why: Medicare dependence 5 creates strong incentive to maximize capped-rental revenue; moderate coding sophistication and limited commercial comparison increase exposure to episode-continuity abuse.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Restarting or duplicating monthly rental revenue, extending payments beyond the applicable cap, avoiding post-cap equipment obligations, or shifting claims to an entity with weaker edits or different operational controls.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: The same beneficiary receives the same or similar capped-rental HCPCS from successive suppliers with overlapping or implausibly adjacent rental months. KH, KI, and KJ sequences restart after supplier changes, or a new supplier bills an initial rental without evidence of remaining months. Claims may show identical equipment descriptions, delivery locations, ordering providers, or beneficiary-contact information across NPIs.
detection_signals: For each beneficiary-HCPCS family, construct a continuous rental episode and flag more than 15 paid rental months absent a documented qualifying interruption or managed-care transition.
Flag a new KH or first-month rental modifier within 60 days of the prior supplier's KJ month or final rental claim.
Flag supplier changes where the replacement supplier bills more months than the calculated remaining months in the episode.
Flag overlapping monthly rental claims from different suppliers for the same or similar HCPCS family.
Flag post-cap rental claims lacking evidence of title status, beneficiary ownership, or the applicable maintenance-and-servicing pathway.
graph_signals: Supplier-to-supplier edges formed by shared beneficiaries, ordering providers, delivery addresses, bank accounts, owners, employees, or equipment serial numbers.
Clusters in which one supplier bills early rental months, another bills later months, and a third bills maintenance after month 15 for the same beneficiary cohort.
Rapid beneficiary migration from one supplier to another immediately following denial spikes or MAC edits.
Shared delivery or warehouse locations inconsistent with independent equipment ownership and service responsibility.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Supplier changes can result from relocation, bankruptcy, network participation changes, service-area restrictions, or beneficiary preference. A legitimate replacement supplier may receive only remaining rental months, and hospital or SNF interruptions can alter anniversary dates.
disambiguating_evidence: Original delivery records, equipment serial numbers, transfer-of-service documentation, and supplier-to-supplier inventory records.
CWF rental-month history and documentation of any qualifying interruption, discharge-date anniversary reset, or managed-care return.
Evidence of the tenth-month purchase-option notice and title transfer where applicable.
Beneficiary confirmation of possession, supplier-change reason, and equipment continuity.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT beneficiary_id, hcpcs_family, COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_npi) AS suppliers, SUM(paid_rental_months) AS total_months, MIN(service_date) AS first_date, MAX(service_date) AS last_date FROM normalized_capped_rental_episodes GROUP BY beneficiary_id, hcpcs_family HAVING total_months > 15 OR COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_npi) >= 2 AND SUM(CASE WHEN rental_modifier IN ('KH','KI','KJ') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > expected_sequence_count;

explicit: Section 30.5.4 - Payments for Capped Rental Items During a Period of Continuous Use
Section 110.4 - Frequency of Claims for Repetitive Services
Section 211.2 - Partial Month Stays for Capped Rental Equipment
cms_source.inference: The continuity rules are explicit. The hypothesis that coordinated entities intentionally fragment episodes and the proposed network linkage are program-integrity inferences.

high_financial_impact.title: Home-Health, Hospice, and DME Supply Boundary Switching
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Section 212 places nonroutine supplies under HHA consolidated billing during an active plan of care but expressly exempts DME, prosthetics, orthotics, and oxygen. Section 140.2 includes HHA supplies in the PPS rate, while Section 10.2 generally bundles DMEPOS furnished to hospice patients unless unrelated to the terminal illness. The boundary between DME, supply, accessory, and unrelated-condition billing can therefore create lifecycle and entity arbitrage.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: It controls or coordinates the plan of care and has direct visibility into HHA episode dates, making the entity boundary financially relevant.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Remote order generation and broad reach can produce DME claims during HHA or hospice periods with limited independent care-setting verification.

archetypes.name: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: High coordination and weak control over beneficiary acquisition can produce parallel HHA, hospice, and supplier billing streams.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: The archetype can distribute claims across HHA, hospice, supplier, and ordering entities to exploit differing bundling rules.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Obtaining separate DMEPOS payment for items potentially included in HHA or hospice payment, or reclassifying supplies and accessories into an exempt or separately payable category.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Supplier claims begin or continue during HHA PPS episodes or hospice election, with HCPCS, POS, and modifiers changing at episode boundaries. Nonroutine supplies may be billed separately by a supplier while the HHA includes related supplies, or oxygen/DME may be billed for a terminal condition without evidence of an unrelated condition. Claims may cluster immediately before HHA admission, after discharge, or around hospice election and revocation.
detection_signals: Flag supplier claims for nonroutine supply codes during active HHA PPS episodes.
Flag DMEPOS claims during hospice enrollment where the diagnosis is related to the terminal condition or no unrelated-condition documentation exists.
Measure abrupt HCPCS/POS/entity changes within 14 days of HHA admission, discharge, hospice election, or revocation.
Identify duplicate or functionally equivalent supply claims across HHA, hospice, and DME supplier entities.
Compare beneficiary-level DME, supply, oxygen, and plan-of-care utilization before, during, and after institutional episodes.
graph_signals: Construct beneficiary-HHA-hospice-supplier-ordering-provider graphs and identify shared ownership, addresses, phone numbers, or referral sources.
Flag HHA or hospice organizations with concentrated referrals to a small group of DME suppliers.
Identify clinicians whose orders drive supplier claims during both hospice and HHA episodes, especially for terminal-condition diagnoses.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: DME, oxygen, prosthetics, and orthotics are legally exempt from HHA consolidated billing. Hospice may separately cover DMEPOS used for a condition unrelated to the terminal illness, and care-setting transitions can legitimately change the billing entity.
disambiguating_evidence: Review the HHA plan of care, consolidated-billing supply list, hospice election diagnosis, terminal prognosis, and unrelated-condition documentation.
Match HCPCS, POS, dates, and revenue codes across HHA, hospice, and supplier claims.
Obtain delivery records and clinical notes showing the item was DME rather than a bundled supply.
Validate episode admission, discharge, hospice election, and revocation dates.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT c.* FROM supplier_claims c LEFT JOIN hha_episodes h ON c.beneficiary_id=h.beneficiary_id AND c.service_date BETWEEN h.start_date AND h.end_date LEFT JOIN hospice_episodes z ON c.beneficiary_id=z.beneficiary_id AND c.service_date BETWEEN z.election_date AND COALESCE(z.revocation_date,DATE '9999-12-31') WHERE (h.beneficiary_id IS NOT NULL AND c.hcpcs IN (SELECT hcpcs FROM nonroutine_hha_supply_list)) OR (z.beneficiary_id IS NOT NULL AND c.condition_related_to_terminal=1 AND c.item_category NOT IN ('EXEMPT_DME','EXEMPT_OXYGEN','EXEMPT_PO'));

10.2 - Coverage Table for DME Claims
140.2 - Billing for HHA Medical Supplies
cms_source.inference: The exemptions and bundling rules are explicit; suspicious classification or diagnosis switching at episode boundaries is an analytic hypothesis.

high_financial_impact.title: Capped-Rental Episode Reset After a Questionable Interruption
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Section 30.5.4 allows a new 15-month capped-rental period only after a break in medical need exceeding 60 days plus the remaining rental-month days, supported by a new prescription, new medical-necessity documentation, and a supplier statement that the prior episode ended. The documentation-based reset creates an opportunity to characterize a temporary interruption, hospitalization, or nonbilling period as a true end of need.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: Its revenue model depends on recurring rental and refill cadence, and its high volume-growth objective and willingness to exploit ambiguity make repeated episode resets economically attractive.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: High volume-growth objective, risk tolerance, beneficiary access, and relatively weak compliance infrastructure support aggressive reuse of lifecycle rules.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: High coordination, Medicare dependence, risk tolerance, and willingness to exploit ambiguity support coordinated documentation and supplier transitions across episodes.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: High coding sophistication and willingness to push technical interpretations make it capable of constructing defensible-looking interruption and restart claims.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Restarting the cap permits additional monthly rental payments for equipment that may be the same or similar to equipment already subject to a completed or partially completed rental period.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: A new capped-rental sequence begins shortly after a prior sequence ends, often with new KH/KI/KJ progression, a new prescription, and a new supplier or billing NPI. The beneficiary may have continuous same-or-similar equipment, uninterrupted diagnosis, no corroborated clinical discontinuation, or only a short inpatient or nonbilling interval. The second episode may involve the same HCPCS, serial number, ordering clinician, address, and delivery channel.
detection_signals: Flag beneficiaries with a second capped-rental start within 180 days of the last rental or ownership event.
Calculate the gap between the last paid rental month and the new episode; prioritize gaps near the regulatory interruption threshold.
Measure the proportion of new episodes supported by an inpatient stay, HHA episode, voluntary nonbilling period, or supplier change rather than documented clinical resolution.
Flag same-or-similar HCPCS restarts with unchanged beneficiary address, ordering provider, diagnosis, and equipment serial number.
Compare episode-reset frequency and paid months per beneficiary against peer suppliers and specialty benchmarks.
graph_signals: Connect sequential suppliers serving the same beneficiary within 12 months, especially where they share ownership, address, bank account, ordering clinicians, or delivery vendors.
Identify ordering providers whose documentation supports unusually high rates of capped-rental restarts across multiple suppliers.
Detect beneficiary clusters receiving episode resets from a common marketer, call center, or referral source.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: A genuine prolonged interruption in medical need, substantial clinical change, loss or irreparable damage, or return from managed care to FFS can create a legitimate new rental context. Administrative nonbilling may also reflect a supplier closure or insurance transition.
disambiguating_evidence: Obtain contemporaneous clinical records showing that medical need actually ended for the required period.
Validate equipment serial numbers, retrieval records, warehouse disposition, and delivery records for the prior and new equipment.
Review the new prescription, physician visit, functional change, and supplier statement required by Section 30.5.4.
Check Medicare Advantage enrollment, inpatient/SNF records, hospice status, and HHA episodes against the claimed interruption.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: WITH episodes AS (SELECT beneficiary_id, supplier_npi, hcpcs, MIN(service_date) AS start_date, MAX(service_date) AS end_date, COUNT(DISTINCT rental_month) AS paid_months FROM claims WHERE payment_status='PAID' AND rental_class='CAPPED' GROUP BY beneficiary_id,supplier_npi,hcpcs,episode_id) SELECT e1.*,e2.* FROM episodes e1 JOIN episodes e2 ON e1.beneficiary_id=e2.beneficiary_id AND e1.hcpcs=e2.hcpcs AND e2.start_date>e1.end_date WHERE e2.start_date-e1.end_date <= 180 AND (e2.supplier_npi<>e1.supplier_npi OR e2.episode_id<>e1.episode_id);

explicit: 30.5.4 - Payments for Capped Rental Items During a Period of Continuous Use
110.4 - Frequency of Claims for Repetitive Services
cms_source.inference: The manual explicitly requires a qualifying break and new documentation; the hypothesis that short or administrative interruptions are mischaracterized is an SIU inference.

high_financial_impact.title: Oxygen Ownership-State and Volume-Modifier Cycling
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 30.6, 30.6.1, and 130.6 distinguish rented versus owned stationary and portable systems, contents fees, portable add-ons, and volume modifiers such as QG, QF, QA, QB, QE, and QR. These mutually exclusive payment paths depend on equipment ownership, prescription flow, and date sequencing, creating an opportunity to cycle states or combine incompatible lines.

archetypes.name: Oxygen/respiratory equipment supplier
archetypes.why: It directly controls equipment inventory, monthly billing, and oxygen recertification workflows; recurring payments and technical modifiers make systematic exploitation plausible.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: High coding sophistication and willingness to exploit ambiguity support manipulation of modifier and ownership-path interpretations.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Broad beneficiary reach and remote order generation make flow-rate, portable-use, and actual equipment possession harder to independently validate.

archetypes.name: Supplier with unusually high Medicare concentration
archetypes.why: Medicare dependence creates strong incentives to maximize every monthly oxygen payment path without commercial-payer cross-checks.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Obtaining both a stationary allowance and a portable add-on or contents fee, securing a 50-percent high-flow increase, or continuing monthly rental after equipment has become owned.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: The same beneficiary has alternating rental and owned-system indicators, incompatible QG/QF or QB/QG combinations, portable add-ons without portable equipment, contents fees while the relevant system is rented or a concentrator is owned, or flow-rate changes clustered around monthly billing dates. Claims may violate the 30-day QG/portable sequencing edits or show repeated new orders without meaningful clinical change.
detection_signals: Flag mutually exclusive oxygen payment combinations within the same calendar month.
Calculate frequency of ownership-status changes by beneficiary and supplier, especially changes occurring near month-end or before a higher-paying modifier.
Flag QG/QB/QF claims without corroborating prescribed flow and portable-system status.
Identify portable add-ons or contents fees inconsistent with the oxygen billing chart for the beneficiary's equipment ownership state.
Measure flow-rate and modifier changes within 30 days of a claim and compare with physician-order changes and test dates.
graph_signals: Link suppliers to ordering providers and testing providers; flag high-volume pairings with repeated high-flow or portable claims.
Identify beneficiaries receiving oxygen from multiple suppliers with conflicting ownership states.
Detect shared equipment serial numbers, delivery vendors, or clinical testing sources across suppliers.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Clinical deterioration, a legitimate change in prescription, transition from rental to ownership, or different stationary and portable systems can produce valid payment-path changes. The manual expressly permits certain combinations based on system ownership and prescribed flow.
disambiguating_evidence: Obtain signed orders, flow-rate prescriptions, arterial blood gas or oximetry results, equipment serial numbers, and delivery/pickup records.
Reconstruct ownership and rental history from supplier records and prior claims.
Apply the oxygen billing chart and 30-day sequencing rules to all lines across suppliers, not only within one claim.
Confirm portable use and whether the beneficiary actually possessed the claimed stationary and portable systems.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT beneficiary_id, service_month FROM oxygen_claims GROUP BY beneficiary_id,service_month HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN modifier IN ('QG','QB','QF') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)>0 AND (SUM(CASE WHEN line_type='portable_addon' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)>0 OR SUM(CASE WHEN line_type='contents' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)>0) AND MAX(CASE WHEN ownership_state_consistent=0 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)=1;

explicit: 30.6 - Oxygen and Oxygen Equipment
30.6.1 - Adjustments to Monthly Oxygen Fee
130.6 - Billing for Oxygen and Oxygen Equipment
130.6.1 - Oxygen Equipment and Contents Billing Chart
cms_source.inference: The ownership and modifier payment paths are explicit; deliberate cycling or incompatible combinations are the analytic interpretation.

high_financial_impact.title: Custom E1399 Versus Standard Orthotic Coding
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: A qualifying customized item is paid as a lump-sum purchase based on individualized cost review and may be billed as E1399 when no specific HCPCS code describes it. However, measurement, fitting, adaptation, or available custom options alone do not qualify. The boundary creates code-path arbitrage between standard L-codes, customized E1399, and physician-ordered P&O billing.

archetypes.name: Orthotics/prosthetics supplier
archetypes.why: High coding sophistication (4) and ambiguity tolerance (4), combined with complex L-code descriptions, make this the most plausible archetype.

archetypes.name: Physician practice dispensing or ordering DME
archetypes.why: The practice controls both ordering and clinical narrative, with beneficiary and referral access scored 5.

archetypes.name: Aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultant
archetypes.why: Coding sophistication (5), ambiguity tolerance (5), and audit awareness (4) support systematic testing of the custom-versus-standard boundary.

archetypes.name: Small independent DME supplier under financial pressure
archetypes.why: High financial pressure (5) and ambiguity tolerance (4) may lead to opportunistic use of a higher-paying custom path despite limited compliance resources.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: A customized-item determination may yield payment based on documented labor, design, fabrication, assembly, and material costs rather than a fixed standard-code fee schedule. Misclassification can increase allowed amounts and reduce the constraints of standard code pricing.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: High E1399 or custom-code utilization; billed charges substantially exceeding comparable standard L-code allowances; repeated use of identical narratives, labor hours, material costs, or construction descriptions across beneficiaries; custom claims without evidence of raw-material fabrication or substantial modification; physician orders that use generic language while claims assert unique construction.
detection_signals: E1399 share of supplier P&O claims compared with specialty peers.
Median allowed amount for E1399 divided by the closest standard L-code allowance.
Duplicate or near-duplicate construction narratives across beneficiaries, measured by text similarity above 0.90.
Custom claims lacking a documented design, fabrication, or labor component.
Percentage of custom claims where billed item features are reused across more than 80% of cases.
graph_signals: Supplier-clinician pairs with unusually high E1399 or custom-code concentration.
Common fabrication vendors, addresses, employees, or narrative templates across multiple suppliers.
Beneficiaries referred by a small network of practices and receiving materially identical custom items.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Some beneficiaries genuinely require unique devices because of unusual anatomy, severe deformity, or complex functional needs. Certain custom-fabricated orthotics also require specialized suppliers and legitimate cost variation.
disambiguating_evidence: Physician description and order specifying the unique construction or substantial modification.
Fabrication worksheet, photographs, measurements, raw-material invoices, labor records, and serial or job numbers.
Comparison with available standard HCPCS descriptors and the beneficiary's clinical condition.
Independent technical review of whether the item could have been appropriately billed under a standard code.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS custom_claims, AVG(allowed_amount / NULLIF(standard_comparator_allowed,0)) AS relative_payment FROM po_claims WHERE hcpcs='E1399' OR custom_indicator=1 GROUP BY supplier_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 15 AND (AVG(allowed_amount / NULLIF(standard_comparator_allowed,0)) > 1.75 OR narrative_similarity_to_prior_claims > 0.90);

explicit: 30.3 - Certain Customized Items
130.4 - Billing for Certain Customized Items
130.1 - Provider Billing for Prosthetic and Orthotic Devices
cms_source.inference: The corpus explicitly distinguishes qualifying customization from fitting or available options; the comparative pricing and narrative-reuse indicators are analytic inferences.

high_financial_impact.title: PEN Pump-Kit-Component Unbundling
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: PEN equipment is rented monthly, nutrients and supplies are purchased, and enteral care kits are all-inclusive. Pump-kit payment is limited when pump documentation is absent, and kit components may not be separately paid. These rules create a code-path opportunity to shift between pump, gravity, kit, and component billing.

archetypes.name: Enteral/parenteral nutrition supplier
archetypes.why: The archetype operates directly in the recurring PEN model, has moderate coding sophistication (3), and is exposed to the direct economic consequences of pump, kit, and nutrient classifications.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: High refill-driven volume objective (4) and ambiguity tolerance (4) make repeated component billing attractive at scale.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Beneficiary reach (5), referral relationships (5), and remote order generation can weaken direct confirmation of administration method and pump necessity.

archetypes.name: Aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultant
archetypes.why: Coding sophistication (5), ambiguity tolerance (5), and audit awareness (4) support systematic use of alternate HCPCS and modifier paths.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: A pump kit or separately billed component path may produce more payment than the documented gravity-fed or all-inclusive kit allowance. Recurring monthly supplies magnify small per-claim differences.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Pump-kit HCPCS appears without compatible pump rental or prescription evidence; gravity-kit and pump-kit codes alternate for the same beneficiary; kit components are billed separately on the same or adjacent dates; nutrient calories, administration method, and equipment codes are inconsistent across certifications and claims.
detection_signals: Percentage of pump-kit claims lacking a paid pump rental, pump purchase, or documented pump order within 90 days.
Component lines billed separately within 30 days of a kit line, normalized by beneficiary and therapy type.
Beneficiaries whose billed administration method changes more than once in 12 months without a revised certification.
Pump-kit utilization above the 95th supplier percentile after adjustment for therapy duration.
Claims where billed calories or units are inconsistent with the current PEN certification.
graph_signals: Supplier-ordering physician pairs with unusually high pump-kit rates.
Repeated beneficiary cohorts sharing the same ordering clinician, certification template, or referral source.
Shared billing staff, address, phone, or ownership between supplier and a nutrition practice.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Patients may legitimately transition between gravity, syringe, and pump administration, and revised clinical prescriptions can lag operational claims. Complex therapy may also require multiple supplies during a transition period.
disambiguating_evidence: Current and prior PEN certifications, prescriptions, and physician progress notes.
Evidence of pump delivery, serial number, maintenance, and actual administration method.
HCPCS component-inclusion table and invoice-level itemization.
Beneficiary or caregiver confirmation of the equipment and supplies received.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT c.supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS suspect_claims FROM pen_claims c LEFT JOIN pen_certifications p ON c.beneficiary_id=p.beneficiary_id AND c.service_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND COALESCE(p.end_date,'9999-12-31') LEFT JOIN pen_pump_claims pump ON c.beneficiary_id=pump.beneficiary_id AND pump.service_date BETWEEN c.service_date-90 AND c.service_date+30 WHERE c.kit_type='pump' AND (p.administration_method <> 'pump' OR pump.claim_id IS NULL OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pen_component_claims x WHERE x.beneficiary_id=c.beneficiary_id AND x.service_date BETWEEN c.service_date-1 AND c.service_date+1 AND x.component_included_in_kit=1)) GROUP BY c.supplier_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10;

30.7.2 - Payment for PEN Supply Kits
100.2.2.2 - Completion of the Elements of PEN CMN
100.2.2.3 - Revised Certifications/Change in Prescription
cms_source.inference: The corpus expressly limits pump-kit payment and prohibits separate payment for included components; the hypothesis is that alternate code paths may be selected to obtain higher payment.

high_financial_impact.title: Repair-Part Versus Maintenance-Servicing Path
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: The corpus uses different payment and modifier paths for RB repair parts, RP non-capped maintenance or repair, and MS capped-rental maintenance. Maintenance of rented equipment is generally bundled, while certain post-cap or owned-equipment servicing is payable. The same physical service can therefore be represented as a repair part, repair, or covered maintenance event with different payment consequences.

archetypes.name: Legitimate high-volume DME supplier
archetypes.why: High volume and mature coding systems (4 compliance and coding sophistication) create scale risk even without aggressive intent.

archetypes.name: Orthotics/prosthetics supplier
archetypes.why: Complex equipment and high ambiguity tolerance (4) make repair-versus-replacement classification difficult and economically significant.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: Coding sophistication (5), ambiguity tolerance (5), and audit awareness (4) support deliberate code-path selection.

archetypes.name: Small independent DME supplier under financial pressure
archetypes.why: Financial pressure (5) and risk tolerance (4) create incentive to bill routine servicing as a separately payable event.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Separately payable repair or maintenance can produce payment where routine servicing is bundled into rental, warranty coverage, or the equipment fee. RB and MS paths may also avoid the limitations applicable to ordinary rental servicing.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: MS claims during active rental months or before the maintenance eligibility date; RP claims for routine checks or cleaning; RB parts billed without a corresponding repair event; repeated repair-part claims at fixed intervals; repair charges exceeding replacement economics; warranty-covered parts billed as Medicare maintenance.
detection_signals: Repair or maintenance claims per equipment unit per year by supplier versus peer percentile.
MS claims occurring before the 13-month or applicable post-cap threshold.
RP or RB claims without a same-day or nearby documented equipment failure or repair labor code.
Repeated identical parts at intervals shorter than expected useful life.
Cumulative repair payments exceeding 50% or 75% of comparable replacement cost.
graph_signals: Supplier-repair-vendor relationships with recurring identical invoices or shared ownership.
Beneficiary clusters linked to one technician, repair facility, or ordering provider.
Shared serial numbers or equipment identifiers across supposedly separate repair events.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Complex equipment can require repeated repairs, and genuine failures may occur during rental. Some capped-rental maintenance fees are payable despite institutionalization, and warranty status may be difficult to reconcile across manufacturers.
disambiguating_evidence: Equipment serial number, service ticket, technician report, parts invoice, and labor documentation.
Warranty and manufacturer coverage records.
Rental, purchase, title, and capped-rental month history.
Clinical or operational evidence that the equipment was rendered unserviceable and required skilled work.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS service_claims, SUM(allowed_amount) AS paid FROM repair_claims r LEFT JOIN equipment_episodes e ON r.beneficiary_id=e.beneficiary_id AND r.equipment_id=e.equipment_id WHERE (r.modifier='MS' AND e.rental_month < 13) OR r.modifier IN ('RP','RB') AND r.service_type IN ('routine_check','cleaning','testing') GROUP BY supplier_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 OR SUM(allowed_amount) > 100000;

40.2 - Maintenance and Service of Capped Rental Items
130.7 - Maintenance and Servicing (Providers and Suppliers)
50.5 - Payment of a Part of a DMEPOS Item
cms_source.inference: The modifier and eligibility distinctions are explicit; the hypothesis is that economically similar servicing events may be assigned to the most favorable payable path.

high_financial_impact.title: HHA-DME Consolidated-Billing Boundary Shifting
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Section 212 subjects nonroutine supplies to home health consolidated billing but expressly exempts DME, prosthetics, orthotics, and oxygen. Sections 110 and 140 provide different HHA and supplier billing routes. A coordinated HHA-supplier network may classify or sequence economically similar items to shift payment between the HHA episode and separate DMEPOS billing, particularly around plan-of-care starts, ends, and gaps.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: The archetype directly controls the boundary between HHA episodes and DMEPOS billing; coordination 4, referral relationships 4, and Medicare dependence 4 support this risk.

archetypes.name: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and beneficiary access 5 can create supplier-HHA referral channels, while compliance sophistication 2 increases risk that consolidated-billing obligations are not reliably checked.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and risk tolerance 5 support intentional division of billing between an HHA and supplier to maximize separate payments.

archetypes.name: Opportunistic individual provider (no initial fraud intent, responds to incentives)
archetypes.why: Low compliance sophistication 2 and moderate willingness to exploit ambiguity 3 make gradual adoption of aggressive HHA-versus-supplier classification plausible without a formal network.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Obtaining separate DMEPOS payment for items otherwise included in the HHA PPS episode, avoiding episode-level payment limits, or increasing total reimbursement by assigning supplies and DME to the entity with the more favorable payment pathway.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Supplier claims for nonroutine supply HCPCS occur during an active 32X or 33X HHA episode, or supplier and HHA claims show overlapping delivery and service periods. Bill type, revenue code, place of service, and HCPCS combinations may alternate around plan-of-care dates. DME or oxygen claims may be legitimate exemptions but show unusually high concentration in the same HHA-supplier relationship.
detection_signals: For each beneficiary, intersect supplier claim dates with HHA episode dates and flag nonroutine supply codes billed separately during active episodes.
Calculate the percentage of a supplier's claims linked to beneficiaries of one or a small number of HHAs; flag concentration above peer benchmarks.

Flag abrupt shifts from HHA revenue code 0270 or PPS billing to supplier DME MAC billing immediately before or after episode boundaries without a corresponding change in HCPCS category or clinical need.
Compare HHA plan-of-care diagnoses, ordered items, and supplier claims; flag same-day or next-day duplicate supply categories.
Flag DME-exempt categories whose utilization increases materially only during active HHA episodes and is concentrated among related entities.
graph_signals: Supplier-HHA pairs with unusually high shared beneficiary volume, shared ownership, addresses, staff, referral providers, or billing vendors.
Ordering providers who refer the same beneficiary to both the HHA and associated DME supplier for overlapping items.
Network communities in which one entity bills supplies during episodes and another bills similar items immediately outside episodes.
Shared delivery records or inventory identifiers between HHA and supplier claims.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: DME, oxygen, prosthetics, and orthotics are expressly exempt from HHA consolidated billing. Beneficiaries may legitimately change clinical needs during an episode, and an HHA may arrange for a supplier to furnish exempt DME.
disambiguating_evidence: The periodically applicable nonroutine-supply code list and the precise HCPCS classification in effect on each date of service.
HHA plan of care, delivery records, physician orders, and documentation identifying whether an item was a consolidated supply or exempt DME.
Ownership and contractual records between the HHA and supplier.
Beneficiary confirmation of the item received and whether it was used as DME or consumed as a routine/nonroutine supply.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT beneficiary_id, supplier_npi, hha_npi, COUNT(*) AS overlapping_claims FROM supplier_claims s JOIN hha_episodes h ON s.beneficiary_id = h.beneficiary_id AND s.service_date BETWEEN h.episode_start AND h.episode_end WHERE s.hcpcs IN (SELECT hcpcs FROM nonroutine_supply_list) GROUP BY beneficiary_id, supplier_npi, hha_npi HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;

explicit: Section 212 - Home Health Consolidated Billing and Supplies Provided by DMEPOS Suppliers
Section 110 - General Billing Requirements
Section 140.2 - Billing for HHA Medical Supplies
cms_source.inference: The distinction between consolidated nonroutine supplies and exempt DME is explicit. The intentional boundary-shifting and network-concentration theory is an inference.

high_financial_impact.title: Oxygen Volume-Modifier and Portable-Add-On Coordination
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 30.6, 100.2.3.1, and 130.6 permit different oxygen payment adjustments based on prescribed flow, daytime/nighttime averages, and portable-equipment status, while expressly prohibiting certain combinations and imposing a 30-day timing edit. A coordinated supplier-ordering network may manipulate or distribute stationary and portable claims, flow-rate documentation, and modifier selection to maximize the applicable add-on or avoid duplicate edits.

archetypes.name: Oxygen/respiratory equipment supplier
archetypes.why: The supplier's core business is monthly oxygen billing, and the rules create recurring, date-driven payment events with direct financial sensitivity to flow-rate and portable status.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Access to beneficiaries 5, referral relationships 5, and geographic reach 5 support remote generation of oxygen orders and distributed documentation across clinicians.

archetypes.name: DME supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: Lead-generation dependence and coordination 5 can produce high-volume oxygen cohorts with standardized prescriptions or fragmented stationary/portable billing.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and risk tolerance 5 support dividing stationary and portable claims or using cooperating clinicians to support high-flow or portable indications.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Obtaining the 50 percent high-flow increase, a portable add-on, or the greater applicable payment while avoiding the no-double-payment and 30-day edits.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: High rates of QG, QB, QF, QR, QA, or QE modifiers; frequent stationary and portable claims near the 30-day edit window; high-flow claims concentrated among a small set of ordering providers or testing facilities. Stationary and portable lines may be billed by different related suppliers, or flow rates may change without corresponding clinical retesting.
detection_signals: Compare each oxygen claim's modifier with the prescribed flow rate, rest/exercise status, daytime/nighttime values, and calculated average; flag mismatches.
Flag QG or QB claims with portable claims in the preceding or following 30 days, including claims split across related suppliers.
Calculate ordering-provider and testing-facility concentration for claims with flow greater than 4 LPM; flag extreme concentration versus peer suppliers.
Flag repeated modifier changes across successive months without a new order, qualifying test, or documented clinical change.
Flag beneficiaries receiving separate stationary and portable equipment claims that conflict with the ownership/rental combinations in the oxygen billing chart.
graph_signals: Ordering providers or testing facilities linked to unusually high proportions of high-flow or portable oxygen beneficiaries across multiple suppliers.
Related suppliers splitting stationary and portable oxygen billing for the same beneficiary or cohort.
Shared marketers, call centers, testing locations, or documentation vendors across high-flow oxygen claims.
Beneficiary clusters with identical flow rates, test dates, diagnoses, and narrative language across different clinicians.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Severe respiratory disease may legitimately require high flow, portable oxygen, or different day/night prescriptions. Beneficiaries may change suppliers, and equipment ownership can change over time.
disambiguating_evidence: Original physician orders, arterial blood gas or oximetry results, testing conditions, and retesting dates.
Equipment delivery, rental, ownership, and portable/stationary system records.
Clinical notes documenting activity-related need or a change in disease severity.
Beneficiary confirmation of actual use and whether both systems were present.

high_financial_impact.title: Lymphedema Component-Code Quantity and Replacement Arbitrage
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: The lymphedema benefit permits multiple body areas and daytime/nighttime garments, with explicit quantity and replacement intervals, while payment can use component, global, or newly priced codes. Component payments may not exceed the original item payment, but new-code pricing can involve claim-by-claim MAC consideration. This creates a code-path opportunity to maximize payment through combinations of component codes, body-area labels, and replacement claims.

archetypes.name: Orthotics/prosthetics supplier
archetypes.why: The supplier has relevant fabrication and coding expertise (coding sophistication 4) and high ambiguity tolerance (4).

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: High volume objective (4), beneficiary access (4), and refill-oriented operations make quantity and replacement rules directly monetizable.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: Growth objective (5) and beneficiary access (4) support high-volume enrollment into a newly expanded benefit.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Beneficiary reach (5), geographic reach (5), and referral relationships (5) facilitate remote identification of diagnoses and body areas.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Component combinations, multiple body-area claims, and early replacement can increase total reimbursement relative to a single global item or compliant replacement cadence. New codes without established pricing may create temporary pricing variability.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: More than three daytime or two nighttime items per body area; RA replacement claims before six months for daytime or two years for nighttime items; simultaneous component and global codes; repeated claims with multiple body-area modifiers or diagnoses not supported by clinical records; allowed amounts exceeding the original item or comparable-code payment.
detection_signals: Quantity per beneficiary, body area, garment type, and rolling 6- or 24-month window.
RA claims occurring before the applicable replacement interval.
Component-plus-global payment ratio by supplier and code family.
Number of distinct body areas billed per beneficiary compared with clinical diagnosis and therapy records.
Supplier-level average allowed amount per lymphedema episode versus national allowed amounts and peers.
graph_signals: Supplier-referral-provider pairs with unusually high multi-body-area or early-replacement rates.
Beneficiary clusters sharing identical measurements, diagnoses, garment sizes, or order language.
Common marketer, call center, fitting location, or shipping address across apparently unrelated suppliers.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Patients may have bilateral or multi-limb disease and can legitimately require both daytime and nighttime garments. Loss, theft, irreparable damage, or changed medical need can justify quantities above ordinary limits or early replacement.
disambiguating_evidence: Authorized-practitioner order and lymphedema diagnosis.
Clinical measurements identifying each body area and garment type.
Proof of loss, damage, changed medical need, or actual replacement of the prior item.
Manufacturer invoice, fitting record, and code-level determination of component versus global billing.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS claims, SUM(allowed_amount) AS paid FROM lymphedema_claims c GROUP BY supplier_id, beneficiary_id, body_area, garment_period HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN garment_period='day' THEN units ELSE 0 END) > 3 OR SUM(CASE WHEN garment_period='night' THEN units ELSE 0 END) > 2 OR SUM(CASE WHEN modifier='RA' AND garment_period='day' AND service_date < prior_delivery_date + INTERVAL '6 months' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) > 0 OR SUM(component_payment) > MAX(original_item_payment);

181.1 - Payment Policy for Lymphedema Compression Treatment Items
cms_source.inference: Quantity, replacement, and component/global pricing limits are explicit; the hypothesis that suppliers may select combinations to maximize payment is an analytic interpretation.

high_financial_impact.title: Upgrade and Purchase-Path Conversion Without Valid ABN or Rental Continuity
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 90 and 120 permit medically appropriate upgrades only with proper beneficiary knowledge and ABN procedures, and require an upgrade to follow the same rental-versus-purchase basis as the medically necessary item. The two-line GA/GZ plus GK structure, or GL for no-charge upgrades, creates a code-path opportunity to bill a more expensive item while obscuring the reasonable-and-necessary baseline or converting a rental obligation into a purchase.

archetypes.name: Orthotics/prosthetics supplier
archetypes.why: Complex item descriptions, customization, and coding discretion make upgrade status difficult to adjudicate from claims alone.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: It has the highest coding sophistication, audit awareness, and willingness to exploit interpretive ambiguity.

archetypes.name: Physician practice dispensing or ordering DME
archetypes.why: It controls the order and can shape documentation supporting the desired configuration, creating a self-referential medical-necessity risk.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: High growth objectives and beneficiary access create incentives to sell higher-priced configurations at scale despite immature ABN controls.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Collecting beneficiary payment for deluxe features, obtaining payment for a higher-priced code, or avoiding the lower rental reimbursement that would apply to the medically necessary item.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Upgraded claims lack the required adjacent GA/GZ and GK lines, use GA without evidence of a valid ABN, bill a purchase when the baseline item would be rented, or show a higher HCPCS without a corresponding reasonable-and-necessary line. Within-code upgrades may have charges that do not correspond to descriptor features. Upgrade patterns may begin after repeated rental months or coincide with equipment replacement.
detection_signals: Flag upgraded claims without the required two adjacent lines and expected modifier pairing.
Flag GA claims with no ABN record, ABN date after delivery, or beneficiary knowledge inconsistent with assignment status.
Flag purchase-path upgrades where the baseline HCPCS is a rental class.
Calculate supplier-level upgrade rates, beneficiary liability, and concentration by ordering provider.
Flag repeated upgrades for the same beneficiary or ordering provider without changed medical need or new equipment features.
graph_signals: Identify ordering providers with unusually high upgrade rates for affiliated or referring suppliers.
Link suppliers and physician practices through ownership, addresses, compensation, or shared staff.
Detect common ABN templates, signatures, or beneficiary contacts across unrelated claims.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: A beneficiary may knowingly request a medically appropriate deluxe item and accept liability after a valid ABN. Suppliers may also provide a higher-quality item at no extra charge using GL, with Medicare paying only the standard item.
disambiguating_evidence: Obtain the signed ABN, assignment status, beneficiary acknowledgment, item make/model, and contemporaneous order.
Verify the baseline item was medically appropriate and that the upgrade remained medically appropriate.
Confirm rental-versus-purchase consistency and the required claim-line sequence.
Review whether the supplier actually collected beneficiary liability and whether the upgrade was provided at no additional charge.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT u.claim_id FROM claims u WHERE u.upgrade_flag=1 AND (NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM claims gk WHERE gk.claim_id=u.claim_id AND gk.modifier='GK') OR (u.modifier='GA' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM abn_records a WHERE a.beneficiary_id=u.beneficiary_id AND a.supplier_npi=u.supplier_npi AND a.signed_date<=u.service_date)) OR (u.baseline_payment_class='RENTAL' AND u.billed_purchase_flag=1));

120 - DME MACs - Billing Procedures Related To ABN Upgrades
120 - Billing Instructions for ABN Upgrades
120.1 - Providing Upgrades of DMEPOS Without Any Extra Charge

high_financial_impact.title: Adaptive Modifier and Code-Path Migration
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 30.3, 120, 120.1, 130.4, and 130.9 provide multiple valid paths for customized, upgraded, rented, purchased, or no-cost upgraded equipment, each with distinct HCPCS and modifier requirements. A supplier using aggressive coding expertise may respond to denials by moving claims between standard codes, E1399, upgrade lines, rental/purchase modifiers, or GL/GA/GZ/GK paths while preserving the underlying economic objective.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: Coding sophistication 5, willingness to exploit ambiguity 5, audit awareness 4, and risk tolerance 4 make adaptive interpretation and rapid post-edit code migration especially plausible.

archetypes.name: Orthotics/prosthetics supplier
archetypes.why: Coding sophistication 4 and willingness to exploit ambiguity 4 make complex customization and code-description boundaries a strong exposure.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: Volume-growth objective 5 and compliance sophistication 2 can lead to implementation of consultant-driven workarounds after denial pressure.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Risk tolerance 5, coordination 5, and willingness to exploit ambiguity 5 support distributing alternate billing paths across entities and clinicians.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Increasing allowed amounts, converting rental economics to purchase economics, collecting upgrade differentials, or preserving payment after a code or modifier edit by shifting to a different defensible claim path.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: After a denial or policy edit, the supplier's mix shifts from a denied HCPCS to E1399, a neighboring code family, or an upgrade structure with adjacent GA/GK lines. Claims may alternate among NU, RR, UE, NR, GL, GA, GZ, and GK in ways inconsistent with equipment lifecycle. Make/model descriptions remain stable while billed HCPCS, purchase status, or customization narratives change.
detection_signals: Use change-point analysis to identify material HCPCS or modifier-mix changes within 30, 60, and 90 days after denial, prepayment review, or audit notification.
For each equipment model or product identifier, calculate the number of HCPCS/modifier pathways used; flag high pathway diversity relative to peers.
Flag claims where line 1 and line 2 do not satisfy the required adjacent upgraded-item structure, or where GA/GZ/GK usage changes without corresponding ABN evidence.
Flag E1399 claims following denials of a specific coded item when make/model, ordering provider, beneficiary, and clinical indication remain materially unchanged.
Compare code-path changes across related suppliers and consultants; flag synchronized changes after a common edit or policy update.
graph_signals: Consultant, billing-vendor, or clearinghouse links shared by suppliers that make synchronized code and modifier changes.
Same ordering providers, beneficiaries, product models, or documentation templates appearing across multiple code paths.
Network entities dividing upgrade, base-item, rental, and purchase lines among separate NPIs.
Shared narrative text, construction-cost schedules, ABN templates, or make/model descriptions across supposedly independent suppliers.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: HCPCS updates, product availability, beneficiary preference, legitimate equipment upgrades, and actual changes in ownership status can require different codes or modifiers. Consultants may lawfully correct systemic billing errors after an edit.
disambiguating_evidence: Product invoices, serial numbers, manufacturer specifications, construction and labor records, and actual equipment delivered.
Valid ABNs, beneficiary election records, assignment status, and evidence that the upgrade remained medically appropriate.
Denial correspondence and internal compliance analyses explaining the code transition.
Ordering-provider records showing a clinically supported change rather than a billing-only reclassification.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: WITH events AS (SELECT supplier_npi, hcpcs_family, denial_date, service_date, billed_hcpcs, modifiers FROM claim_events) SELECT supplier_npi, COUNT(DISTINCT billed_hcpcs) AS post_denial_codes, COUNT(DISTINCT modifier_signature) AS post_denial_paths FROM events WHERE service_date BETWEEN denial_date AND denial_date + INTERVAL '90 days' GROUP BY supplier_npi HAVING post_denial_codes >= 3 OR post_denial_paths >= 4;
