Section 120 - General Instructions for ABN Upgrades
Section 120 - Billing Instructions for ABN Upgrades
Section 130.4 - Billing for Certain Customized Items
Section 130.9 - Showing Whether Rented or Purchased
cms_source.inference: The alternative billing paths and required modifiers are explicit. Adaptive migration after denials and shared consultant influence are analytic inferences.

high_financial_impact.title: Low-and-Slow Cross-Entity Replacement and Accessory Accumulation
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 10.2, 30.3, 40.1, 50, 50.1, 50.5, and 181 permit separately payable repairs, replacement parts, customized items, replacement equipment, and lymphedema garments subject to ownership, useful-lifetime, quantity, or medical-necessity rules. Individual claims may be below simple thresholds, but a distributed network can accumulate excessive accessories, repairs, replacements, and body-area-specific items over time.

archetypes.name: Orthotics/prosthetics supplier
archetypes.why: Coding sophistication 4 and willingness to exploit ambiguity 4 support technically defensible segmentation of custom items, parts, repairs, and replacements.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: The business model is built around repeated accessory and replacement revenue, with volume-growth objective 4 and audit awareness 2.

archetypes.name: Legitimate high-volume DME supplier
archetypes.why: Scale and geographic reach 4 can create material exposure even from small error rates; this is a lower-intent risk requiring control calibration rather than a presumption of fraud.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and risk tolerance 5 support distributing individually plausible claims across suppliers and beneficiaries to remain below single-entity thresholds.

archetypes.name: Opportunistic individual provider (no initial fraud intent, responds to incentives)
archetypes.why: Low compliance sophistication 2 and willingness to exploit ambiguity 3 fit gradual normalization of frequent replacement or accessory billing after observing low denial rates.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Generating recurring revenue from parts, repairs, garments, and replacements while avoiding single-claim quantity or frequency thresholds and spreading utilization across entities.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: A beneficiary receives multiple related accessories, repairs, replacement parts, or lymphedema garments from different suppliers over a long period. Claims individually comply with quantity limits but collectively exceed expected useful life, replacement intervals, or clinical need. RB, RP, MS, RA, and custom-item pathways may alternate without clear equipment lifecycle progression.
detection_signals: Aggregate claims by beneficiary, equipment family, body area, and network rather than by NPI; flag cumulative quantities exceeding section-specific limits or peer distributions.
Calculate time from original delivery to replacement and compare with useful-lifetime, six-month, two-year, or eight-year rules where applicable.
Flag repeated repair-part claims within 90 days of a replacement or purchase claim, and repeated repairs whose cumulative allowed amount approaches or exceeds replacement cost.
Flag lymphedema claims exceeding three daytime or two nighttime items per body area, or replacements earlier than six months or two years without documented exception.
Flag low-frequency patterns such as one accessory or repair every few months that become anomalous over 24-36 months.
graph_signals: Beneficiary-level accumulation spread across suppliers sharing ordering providers, addresses, owners, fulfillment centers, or marketers.
Supplier networks where one entity bills the base item, another bills RB repair parts, and another bills replacement or accessory items.
Ordering providers with repeated replacement claims for the same equipment family across many suppliers.
Shared equipment serial numbers, product models, or clinical narratives across ostensibly independent claims.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Complex or progressive conditions may require multiple body areas, repairs, replacements after loss or damage, and different accessories. High-volume suppliers may serve medically complex populations and legitimately distribute claims across branches.
disambiguating_evidence: Equipment inventory and serial-number history, delivery and return records, warranty coverage, and repair work orders.
Clinical documentation supporting changed medical need, loss, irreparable damage, or body-area-specific lymphedema treatment.
Beneficiary confirmation of possession, damage, replacement, and actual use.
Ownership, referral, and fulfillment relationships among suppliers in the beneficiary's claim history.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT beneficiary_id, equipment_family, SUM(units) AS cumulative_units, COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_npi) AS suppliers, COUNT(*) AS claims, MIN(service_date) AS first_date, MAX(service_date) AS last_date FROM dme_accessory_replacement_claims GROUP BY beneficiary_id, equipment_family HAVING (cumulative_units > peer_99th_percentile_units OR suppliers >= 3 AND claims >= 6) AND DATEDIFF(day, first_date, last_date) >= 365;

Section 40.1 - General maintenance and service
Section 50 - Payment for Replacement of Equipment
Section 50.1 - Payment for Replacement of Capped Rental Items
Section 181 - Lymphedema Compression Treatment Benefit
cms_source.inference: The individual coverage, replacement, and quantity rules are explicit. Longitudinal aggregation across entities and low-and-slow accumulation are analytic inferences.

high_financial_impact.title: HHA-versus-DME-MAC Supply Routing
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: The corpus exempts DME, prosthetics, orthotics, and oxygen from home-health consolidated billing, while nonroutine medical supplies remain bundled during an HH PPS episode. The same beneficiary need can therefore follow materially different billing paths depending on whether it is characterized as DME, a DME accessory, or an HHA supply.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: High referral and coordination scores (4 each) and direct access to plan-of-care information create the ability to influence whether an item is furnished through the HHA or routed to a supplier.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: High growth objective (5), beneficiary access (4), and willingness to exploit ambiguity (4) support aggressive acquisition of HHA-associated DME volume.

archetypes.name: Supplier heavily dependent on lead-generation companies
archetypes.why: High beneficiary reach and coordination (5 each) make it plausible that outsourced lead sources steer beneficiaries toward separately billed supplier channels.

archetypes.name: Opportunistic individual provider (no initial fraud intent, responds to incentives)
archetypes.why: Low compliance and coding sophistication (2 each) makes misunderstanding the DME-versus-supply boundary plausible, with drift toward the more remunerative billing path.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Separate supplier billing can create payment outside the HHA PPS episode, whereas comparable nonroutine supplies may be absorbed into the HHA payment. Routing volume to the supplier can also shift beneficiary acquisition credit and revenue away from the HHA.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Supplier claims for DME, accessories, oxygen, or related supplies overlap an active HHA episode, while HHA claims show the same patient, diagnosis, plan-of-care activity, or equipment need. The pattern may include supplier claims for items on the periodically published nonroutine-supply lists, inconsistent HHA bill types, or supplier and HHA claims for the same episode.
detection_signals: Rate of supplier DMEPOS claims during active HH PPS episodes compared with peer suppliers: flag rates above the 95th percentile.
Percentage of supplier beneficiaries with overlapping HHA episodes and the same or related diagnosis within 7 days: flag above 50%.
Supplier claims for codes listed as HH nonroutine supplies during HH episodes, with paid amount greater than zero.
Same-beneficiary HHA and supplier claims for the same HCPCS family within 1, 3, and 7 days.
Change-point analysis showing increased supplier billing after an HHA referral, ownership, or contracting change.
graph_signals: Dense supplier-HHA-beneficiary triads with repeated referrals involving the same ordering clinicians.
Shared ownership, address, phone, bank account, or enrollment contacts between the HHA and supplier.
Beneficiaries concentrated among a small set of HHA episodes or ordering providers relative to the supplier's broader panel.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: DME, prosthetics, orthotics, and oxygen are expressly exempt from HH consolidated billing. A supplier may legitimately furnish exempt DME while the HHA separately furnishes bundled supplies. Transitional discharge needs and different clinical suppliers can also generate close dates.
disambiguating_evidence: HCPCS-level determination of whether each item is exempt DME or a bundled nonroutine supply.
HHA plan of care, ordered equipment, delivery records, and documentation identifying the responsible furnishing entity.
Evidence that the item was actually delivered and used at home rather than supplied as part of an HHA visit.
Contracting and ownership records showing whether the HHA and supplier are independent.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: WITH active_hh AS (SELECT beneficiary_id, start_date, end_date FROM hh_episodes WHERE status='active') SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS claims, SUM(paid_amount) AS paid FROM dmepos_claims c JOIN active_hh h ON c.beneficiary_id=h.beneficiary_id AND c.service_date BETWEEN h.start_date AND h.end_date WHERE c.hcpcs IN (nonroutine_supply_list UNION exempt_dme_list) GROUP BY supplier_id HAVING SUM(CASE WHEN c.hcpcs IN (nonroutine_supply_list) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(*),0) > 0.25 OR COUNT(DISTINCT c.beneficiary_id) > peer_percentile(95);

explicit: 212 - Home Health Consolidated Billing and Supplies Provided by DMEPOS Suppliers
110.2 - Application of DMEPOS Fee Schedule
140.2 - Billing for HHA Medical Supplies
cms_source.inference: The corpus explicitly defines exempt DME and bundled nonroutine supplies; the abuse hypothesis is that entity selection and item characterization may be used to move economically similar services between those paths.

high_financial_impact.title: Anniversary-Date Harvesting Around Hospital or SNF Discharge
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 210 and 211.2 permit a full capped-rental month when the beneficiary is home on the from or anniversary date, including when that date is discharge. If an inpatient stay overlaps the anniversary date, discharge becomes the new anniversary date. The from-date-only crossover edit can leave payment dependent on precise claim dating and discharge timing.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: It operates at the home/institution boundary and has access to admission, discharge, and plan-of-care information, while coordination risk and Medicare dependence increase exposure.

archetypes.name: Skilled nursing facility-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: SNF admission and discharge data directly control the anniversary-date outcome, creating a strong opportunity for timing-sensitive billing behavior.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: High coordination and risk tolerance support deliberate alignment of claim dates, discharge information, and supplier billing.

archetypes.name: Oxygen/respiratory equipment supplier
archetypes.why: Its recurring monthly rental model and date-driven billing make full-month payment around institutional transitions financially material.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Preserving or restarting a full monthly rental payment despite an institutional stay, and avoiding an unpaid month or lost rental month.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Capped-rental claims use discharge dates as new from dates, show abrupt anniversary-date shifts, or receive a full monthly allowance despite only a brief home period. Claims may be submitted soon after discharge with annotations, while inpatient or SNF records show conflicting admission/discharge dates, overlapping supplier claims, or no evidence the equipment was at home.
detection_signals: Calculate the percentage of capped-rental claims with a from date equal to an inpatient or SNF discharge date.
Flag full-month payments where home days on the anniversary date are supported only by same-day discharge and no home-delivery or possession evidence exists.
Measure claim resubmission and date-change rates within 30 days of inpatient or SNF denials.
Flag suppliers with unusually high proportions of anniversary-date changes, discharge-date claims, or paid claims immediately following institutional stays.
Compare rental-month sequence and KH/KI/KJ modifiers before and after every anniversary-date reset.
graph_signals: Link suppliers to facilities with unusually high shared beneficiary discharge-date claims.
Identify facility discharge planners, ordering providers, or DME liaisons associated with abnormal concentrations of discharge-date rental claims.
Detect sequential suppliers billing the same beneficiary on the same discharge date or sharing delivery documentation.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: A beneficiary may legitimately be home on the discharge date and entitled to a full rental month under the explicit policy. Hospitalizations that overlap an anniversary date can legitimately require a new anniversary date.
disambiguating_evidence: Validate facility admission and discharge timestamps, discharge destination, and whether the destination was a qualified home-like setting.
Obtain delivery, possession, and home-use records for the equipment on the claimed from date.
Review original delivery date, rental-month sequence, claim annotations, and CWF adjudication history.
Exclude claims where the beneficiary was discharged to another inpatient or SNF facility rather than home.

high_financial_impact.title: Maintenance-and-Servicing Substitution During Rental or Institutional Care
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 40.1 and 130.7 generally prohibit maintenance and servicing while equipment is rented, while Section 210/211 permits capped-rental maintenance claims with modifier MS even when the beneficiary is institutionalized. This creates a code-path and timing collision in which repair, replacement-part, maintenance, or MS claims may be used to obtain payment for costs already included in rental or facility responsibility.

archetypes.name: Oxygen/respiratory equipment supplier
archetypes.why: Equipment is recurring and service-intensive, and institutional stays are common, creating repeated opportunities to classify routine service as separately payable maintenance.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: Its operational model and high refill volume can blur the distinction between replacement accessories, repair parts, and routine servicing.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: It operates across home and institutional settings and has elevated coordination risk with facilities and caregivers.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination across supplier, facility, and beneficiary records can support distributed repair and maintenance billing.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Collecting separate payment for routine service, parts, delivery, or maintenance that should be included in rental, warranty, PPS, or the capped-rental maintenance allowance.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: MS or RP claims appear during active rental months, during inpatient/SNF stays, or shortly after delivery. The same date may include rental, repair part RB, replacement accessory, and maintenance lines. Claims may lack evidence of an actual repair incident, contain repeated low-dollar services, or show parts inconsistent with the base equipment.
detection_signals: Flag MS/RP/RB claims during active rental periods except explicitly payable capped-rental maintenance circumstances.
Flag maintenance claims during inpatient or SNF stays and compare with equipment possession and facility responsibility.
Calculate repair and maintenance frequency per equipment-month and supplier-level outlier rates.
Identify same-day or near-day rental plus MS/RP/RB combinations for the same HCPCS or serial number.
Flag maintenance payments within warranty periods or without documented labor, part, and incident records.
graph_signals: Link suppliers to repair vendors, facilities, and manufacturers; identify common ownership or billing addresses.
Detect repeated repair claims across beneficiaries using the same equipment serial-number family or service technician.
Identify facilities whose stays are associated with unusually high supplier MS/RP activity.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: A genuine repair may be payable for beneficiary-owned equipment, and capped-rental MS fees have specific exceptions. Equipment can require necessary servicing during an institutional stay, and warranty status may be incorrectly recorded.
disambiguating_evidence: Verify rental, ownership, warranty, and capped-rental month status.
Obtain work orders, technician notes, parts invoices, serial numbers, and proof that the repair actually occurred.
Determine whether the charge is a covered capped-rental maintenance fee, an actual repair part, or a nonpayable routine service.
Review facility records to establish who supplied and was responsible for the equipment during the stay.

high_financial_impact.title: Useful-Lifetime and Same-or-Similar Replacement Acceleration
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Section 50.1 measures useful lifetime from delivery to the beneficiary, not manufacture or acquisition date, and permits replacement after useful lifetime or loss/irreparable damage. Sections 30.5.4 and 50 also state that supplier changes and different but similar equipment do not automatically create new rental periods. These rules create opportunities to characterize early replacement, supplier transfer, or an upgrade as a qualifying replacement event.

archetypes.name: Orthotics/prosthetics supplier
archetypes.why: Its coding sophistication and high willingness to exploit ambiguity make nuanced replacement, customization, and same-or-similar distinctions attractive.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: It has the highest coding sophistication and ambiguity tolerance, enabling technical arguments about useful lifetime, configuration, and replacement basis.

archetypes.name: Multi-state supplier
archetypes.why: Geographic reach enables routing replacement activity across jurisdictions and billing entities, complicating lifecycle matching.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordinated suppliers and clinicians can distribute original, replacement, and ownership events across entities.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Obtaining a new purchase or rental stream before the prior item reaches its useful lifetime, or converting a similar-item change into a separately payable replacement or accessory episode.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Replacement claims occur before the beneficiary-specific useful lifetime, use RA or replacement indicators inconsistently, or follow a supplier change without a documented transfer of rental months. New equipment may have the same HCPCS, serial number, diagnosis, ordering provider, or functional purpose as prior equipment. A higher-priced configuration may be billed as replacement without evidence of changed medical need, loss, or irreparable damage.
detection_signals: Calculate elapsed time from verified delivery of the prior item to each replacement claim and flag intervals below the MAC-established useful lifetime.
Flag same-or-similar HCPCS replacements within 60 months absent documented loss, irreparable damage, or substantial clinical change.
Identify replacements where the prior item has active rental payments or ownership status and no retrieval, destruction, theft, or damage record.
Compare replacement rates by supplier, ordering provider, beneficiary cohort, and HCPCS against peer distributions.
Flag replacement claims with changed supplier but unchanged serial number, address, diagnosis, and equipment configuration.
graph_signals: Link old and new suppliers through common ownership, addresses, employees, warehouse locations, or ordering providers.
Track equipment serial numbers across suppliers and beneficiaries.
Identify clinician-supplier pairs with unusually high rates of early replacements or upgraded replacements.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Items may be lost, stolen, irreparably damaged, or rendered inadequate by a genuine change in condition. Supplier bankruptcy or service failure can also require replacement under specific rules.
disambiguating_evidence: Obtain delivery date, serial number, title records, repair history, damage reports, police or loss documentation, and retrieval records.
Review current physician order and clinical documentation for changed medical need.
Validate supplier bankruptcy or court records when that exception is invoked.
Compare the replacement configuration with the prior item and assess whether it is truly different or merely similar.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT r.* FROM replacement_claims r JOIN equipment_history h ON r.beneficiary_id=h.beneficiary_id AND r.same_similar_group=h.same_similar_group WHERE r.service_date < h.prior_delivery_date + INTERVAL '60 months' AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM replacement_evidence e WHERE e.claim_id=r.claim_id AND e.reason IN ('LOSS','IRREPARABLE_DAMAGE','CHANGED_CONDITION','BANKRUPTCY'));

explicit: 50 - Payment for Replacement of Equipment
50.1 - Payment for Replacement of Capped Rental Items
30.5.4 - Payments for Capped Rental Items During a Period of Continuous Use
cms_source.inference: The manual states the replacement and same-or-similar rules; the proposed early-replacement pattern is an analytic hypothesis.

high_financial_impact.title: PEN Pump Reset Through Therapy-Type or Two-Month Break Coding
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 30.7.1 and 100.2.2.1 end PEN medical need after two consecutive months without medically necessary services and permit a new rental period only with a documented break. A prescription change between parenteral and enteral nutrients is an exception to the no-additional-rental rule. The combination may permit a continuing therapy program to be represented as a new therapy type or interrupted episode.

archetypes.name: Enteral/parenteral nutrition supplier
archetypes.why: It controls recurring pump rentals, nutrients, and certification workflows, and the therapy-type distinction directly affects its revenue stream.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: It sees therapy changes and care-setting transitions, with coordination across HHA, physician, and supplier records.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: Technical sophistication and high ambiguity tolerance support exploiting the distinction between prescription changes and genuine medical-need termination.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Multiple parties can coordinate prescriptions, supplier changes, and claims to create apparent therapy breaks.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Obtaining additional pump rental months beyond the 15-month limit or restarting a pump rental after a purported two-month end of medical need.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: A new pump rental sequence follows two months with no pump or nutrient claims, but clinical records show ongoing nutrition support, supplies continue, or the beneficiary retains the same pump. Alternatively, enteral-to-parenteral or parenteral-to-enteral transitions occur without corresponding clinical documentation, while the same equipment and supplier continue billing.
detection_signals: Flag new 15-month pump episodes following exactly two or three months without pump claims but with ongoing PEN nutrients, supplies, HHA visits, or nutrition-related diagnoses.
Flag therapy-type changes unsupported by a revised certification, new physician order, or clinical event.
Identify pump rentals beyond 15 cumulative months by beneficiary and equipment family across suppliers.
Compare pump, nutrient, kit, and certification timelines for gaps and inconsistent therapy states.
Flag supplier changes that coincide with the apparent break but show continuous equipment possession or unchanged delivery location.
graph_signals: Link suppliers, ordering physicians, dietitians, HHAs, and facilities around therapy transitions.
Identify clinicians associated with unusually high enteral/parenteral switching or pump resets.
Track the same pump serial number across supposed new episodes and suppliers.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: A real change in nutritional route, hospitalization, temporary voluntary nonbilling, or clinically documented cessation of nutrients can legitimately affect the rental period. Section 30.7.1 specifically recognizes a prescription change between parenteral and enteral nutrients.
disambiguating_evidence: Obtain nutrition notes, hospitalization records, revised certifications, prescriptions, dietitian assessments, and evidence of the actual two-month cessation.
Verify whether nutrients were medically necessary and furnished during the alleged break.
Match pump serial number, possession, maintenance, and delivery records across episodes.
Confirm that the therapy change was clinically real rather than a billing-only classification.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT p.* FROM pen_pump_episodes p JOIN pen_history h ON p.beneficiary_id=h.beneficiary_id WHERE p.start_date > h.last_episode_end AND p.start_date-h.last_episode_end BETWEEN 60 AND 150 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pen_claims x WHERE x.beneficiary_id=p.beneficiary_id AND x.service_date BETWEEN h.last_episode_end AND p.start_date AND x.category IN ('NUTRIENT','SUPPLY','HHA_NUTRITION')) AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM certifications z WHERE z.beneficiary_id=p.beneficiary_id AND z.effective_date<=p.start_date AND z.documents_true_break=1);

explicit: 30.7.1 - Payment for Parenteral and Enteral Pumps
100.2.2.1 - Scheduling and Documenting Certifications and Recertifications of Medical Necessity for PEN
100.2.2.3 - Revised Certifications/Change in Prescription
cms_source.inference: The two-month termination and therapy-change exception are explicit; using unrelated continuing claims to identify false breaks is an SIU inference.

high_financial_impact.title: Pre-Discharge Delivery Date-of-Service Inflation
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Pre-discharge delivery is permitted for home-use DME, prosthetics, and orthotics only under narrow fitting and training conditions, with the discharge date generally serving as the claim date and no payment for pre-discharge days. The distinction between facility delivery, fitting, caregiver possession, and actual home delivery creates a place-of-service and date-of-service vulnerability.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: High beneficiary access (4), referral relationships (4), and growth objective (5) encourage discharge-day acquisition and rapid processing.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Geographic reach (5) and beneficiary access (5) make remote order generation and weak physical verification more likely.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: The provider operates at the transition boundary and has coordination (4) with discharge and home-health staff.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: High coordination (5) and beneficiary access (5) support synchronized facility, supplier, and beneficiary documentation.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Backdating or treating facility fitting as home delivery can create an additional payable rental or purchase date, avoid inpatient bundling, or support a new rental episode earlier than allowed.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: DME claims dated before discharge, delivery records showing facility addresses without home delivery, claims on discharge dates despite discharge to another inpatient or SNF, rental periods beginning before the beneficiary's actual home receipt, or multiple suppliers reporting delivery for the same transition.
detection_signals: Claims with service dates 1-2 days before inpatient discharge.
Percentage of pre-discharge claims lacking a qualified home-like discharge destination.
Delivery address mismatch between claim, supplier proof of delivery, and beneficiary residence.
Rental first-month claims with a date earlier than discharge or actual home delivery.
Multiple delivery or fitting events from different suppliers within 3 days of discharge.
graph_signals: Repeated supplier-discharge-planner or supplier-facility relationships with unusually high pre-discharge utilization.
Shared clinicians or referral sources between the supplier and facility.
Beneficiary clusters receiving identical equipment on facility discharge dates.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: The manual expressly permits pre-discharge fitting and training within two days before discharge when the item is medically necessary for home use and reaches the home on discharge. Caregiver transport and facility-leave arrangements can produce legitimate date discrepancies.
disambiguating_evidence: Discharge destination, discharge summary, and actual home-delivery timestamp.
Proof of delivery signed by beneficiary or caregiver at the home address.
Fitting and training records showing the qualifying two-day window.
Evidence that the facility did not shift its inpatient obligation to the supplier.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS pre_discharge_claims FROM dmepos_claims c JOIN inpatient_stays s ON c.beneficiary_id=s.beneficiary_id AND c.service_date BETWEEN s.discharge_date-2 AND s.discharge_date WHERE c.service_date < s.discharge_date OR c.delivery_address_type='facility' GROUP BY supplier_id HAVING COUNT(*) >= 10 OR SUM(CASE WHEN c.service_date < s.discharge_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / NULLIF(COUNT(*),0) > 0.10;

explicit: 110.3.1 - Conditions That Must Be Met
110.3.2 - Date of Service for Pre-Discharge Delivery of DMEPOS
110.3.3 - Facility Responsibilities During the Transition Period
cms_source.inference: The permitted scenarios and date rules are explicit; the abuse hypothesis concerns misreporting facility fitting or delivery as qualifying home delivery.

high_financial_impact.title: Pre-Discharge Delivery Converted Into Premature or Duplicate Billing
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 110.3.1 and 110.3.2 allow pre-discharge delivery of DME, prosthetics, or orthotics for fitting or training within two days before discharge, but the date of service is generally discharge or later home delivery, and no pre-discharge day is separately billable. The distinction between fitting delivery, deemed delivery, and actual home delivery can be operationally difficult to validate.

archetypes.name: Physician practice dispensing or ordering DME
archetypes.why: It controls both the order and beneficiary access, making it capable of coordinating fitting documentation with equipment billing.

archetypes.name: Rapidly growing DME supplier
archetypes.why: High growth objectives and access to beneficiaries create incentives to deliver early and bill quickly, while compliance build-out may lag operations.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Geographic reach and decoupled order generation make physical delivery, fitting, and home use harder to independently verify.

archetypes.name: Skilled nursing facility-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: It has direct access to facility discharge timelines and can influence whether an item is characterized as training, facility equipment, or home equipment.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Accelerating claim submission, obtaining payment for equipment associated with an inpatient stay, or duplicating facility and supplier payment for the same item.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Claims use delivery or fitting dates before discharge, duplicate lines for the same HCPCS around discharge, home POS inconsistent with facility records, or separate delivery charges despite the prohibition. The item may remain at the facility after discharge, be removed and later redelivered, or appear on both a facility and supplier claim.
detection_signals: Flag DME/P&O claims with service dates one or two days before discharge.
Flag claims where the billed date is earlier than both discharge and verified home delivery.
Calculate duplicate or near-duplicate HCPCS/serial-number claims within 14 days of discharge across facility and supplier bill types.
Flag pre-discharge claims with no discharge to home-like POS within two days.
Measure separate delivery-charge frequency on pre-discharge cases and compare with peers.
graph_signals: Match suppliers to facilities, discharge planners, and ordering clinicians with repeated pre-discharge billing.
Identify common serial numbers or item identifiers across facility and supplier claims.
Detect suppliers receiving referrals from facilities where nearly all deliveries occur immediately before discharge.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Fitting and training before discharge are expressly permitted when the equipment is medically necessary for home use and delivered within the permitted window. Some facilities may document the item as left at the facility and taken home by the caregiver on discharge.
disambiguating_evidence: Verify discharge destination, caregiver acknowledgment, home-delivery or pickup records, and item serial number.
Review fitting/training notes, physician order, initial need date, and exact delivery chronology.
Check whether the facility was responsible for a similar item during the stay and whether any facility claim included the equipment.
Confirm that the claim date follows the deemed-delivery rules in Section 110.3.2.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT c.* FROM claims c JOIN inpatient_stays s ON c.beneficiary_id=s.beneficiary_id WHERE c.item_category IN ('DME','P&O') AND c.service_date BETWEEN s.discharge_date-INTERVAL '2 day' AND s.discharge_date-INTERVAL '1 day' OR (c.service_date<s.discharge_date AND c.paid_amount>0);

explicit: 110.3.1 - Conditions That Must Be Met
110.3.2 - Date of Service for Pre-Discharge Delivery of DMEPOS
110.3.3 - Facility Responsibilities During the Transition Period
cms_source.inference: The manual explicitly defines allowable pre-discharge activity; premature billing, duplicate billing, and unsupported home delivery are detection hypotheses.

high_financial_impact.title: Jurisdiction and Billing-Entity Arbitrage
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 10, 20.2, 30, 110, 130.1, and 160 assign DMEPOS claims to different contractors or claim formats based on supplier location, beneficiary residence, HCPCS category, institutional status, and whether the item is implanted, PEN, P&O, or DME. A multi-state or multi-entity network may exploit these routing differences to move economically similar claims among billing entities or jurisdictions with differing edits and documentation practices.

archetypes.name: Multi-state supplier
archetypes.why: Geographic reach 5 and explicit ability to route activity across jurisdictions create the strongest structural basis for entity and jurisdiction arbitrage.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and geographic reach 4 support routing claims through cooperating entities while maintaining a common beneficiary or referral pipeline.

archetypes.name: Supplier using aggressive coding/revenue-cycle consultants
archetypes.why: Coding sophistication 5, audit awareness 4, and willingness to exploit ambiguity 5 support deliberate identification of alternate HCPCS, contractor, or institutional billing paths.

archetypes.name: Telehealth-linked DME supplier
archetypes.why: Geographic reach 5 and referral relationships 5 allow remote ordering and fulfillment across multiple jurisdictions, although the pattern requires a multi-entity or multi-state operating structure.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Obtaining payment under a more favorable contractor pathway, avoiding a jurisdiction-specific edit, accessing an alternative fee schedule or claim format, or reducing documentation friction for an economically similar item.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Related claims for similar products appear under supplier versus HHA, hospital, SNF, or physician-associated entities; implanted-DME accessories route to A/B MAC (B), while other DME routes to a DME MAC. New or reclassified HCPCS codes shift abruptly between contractor jurisdictions. Supplier location, beneficiary residence, ordering-provider location, place of service, and delivery address are inconsistent or unusually distant.
detection_signals: Calculate the proportion of a supplier's claims routed to each MAC and compare with expected jurisdiction based on supplier location, beneficiary residence, HCPCS, and provider type.
Flag economically similar HCPCS families where the same network bills different entities or claim formats within 30 days for comparable beneficiaries.
Flag supplier-to-beneficiary delivery distances above the 99th percentile, especially when local suppliers exist and separate delivery charges are claimed.
Flag abrupt increases in claims for codes newly assigned to A/B MAC jurisdiction or changes in billing entity immediately after a denial or edit.
Compare paid amounts and denial rates for the same HCPCS family across related entities and jurisdictions; flag material divergence unexplained by beneficiary residence.
graph_signals: Shared ownership, addresses, bank accounts, officers, employees, fulfillment facilities, ordering providers, or referral marketers across entities billing different MACs.
Cross-jurisdiction beneficiary migration in which the same marketer or ordering provider feeds multiple supplier NPIs.
Network paths connecting one clinician to multiple billing entities that alternate by HCPCS category or contractor jurisdiction.
Entity pairs with unusually high claim substitution: one entity bills DME while another bills implanted accessories, PEN, P&O, or HHA versions for overlapping beneficiaries.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Legitimate multi-state suppliers may centralize billing while serving beneficiaries nationwide. Contractor jurisdiction genuinely varies by HCPCS, provider type, implanted status, and beneficiary or supplier location; fee schedules and code assignments also change over time.
disambiguating_evidence: Enrollment records, ownership disclosures, service locations, state licenses, and actual fulfillment locations.
Purchase orders, delivery records, equipment serial numbers, and documentation showing the correct benefit category and billing entity.
MAC jurisdiction files and effective-date histories for HCPCS assignments.
Contractual arrangements explaining shared administrative services without shared clinical or billing control.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT network_id, hcpcs_family, COUNT(DISTINCT mac_id) AS macs, COUNT(DISTINCT billing_entity_type) AS entity_types, AVG(delivery_distance_miles) AS avg_distance FROM claims_enriched WHERE paid_flag = 1 GROUP BY network_id, hcpcs_family HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT mac_id) >= 2 OR COUNT(DISTINCT billing_entity_type) >= 3 AND AVG(delivery_distance_miles) > 200;

explicit: Section 10 - Where to Bill DMEPOS and PEN Items and Services
Section 20.2 - Locality
Section 110 - General Billing Requirements
Section 160.1 - Billing for TPN and EN Furnished to Part B Inpatients
cms_source.inference: The routing and locality rules are explicit. The inference is that related entities may deliberately select pathways based on operational payment or edit differences.

high_financial_impact.title: Discharge-Date and Anniversary-Date Cycling
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 110.3, 210, and 211.2 permit full-month DME payment when the beneficiary is home on the from or anniversary date and allow a capped-rental anniversary date to reset to a discharge date when an inpatient stay overlaps that date. Coordinated suppliers may exploit repeated transitions among home, hospital, and SNF settings or inconsistent date reporting to create paymentable months while obscuring continuous use.

archetypes.name: Skilled nursing facility-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: The archetype operates directly at admission and discharge boundaries, with coordination 4 and access to beneficiaries 4; timing-sensitive billing is a natural exposure.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: Home-based care and transition coordination create access to discharge information, while referral relationships 4 and coordination 4 support billing around return-to-home dates.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and risk tolerance 5 support deliberate synchronization of claims, discharge dates, and supplier changes.

archetypes.name: Oxygen/respiratory equipment supplier
archetypes.why: Oxygen is billed monthly and has high recurring revenue; access to beneficiaries 4 and Medicare dependence 4 make hospitalization and discharge timing especially material.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Preserving a full monthly rental payment, creating additional payable rental months, or restarting or extending rental revenue after a hospitalization or SNF stay.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Capped-rental claims repeatedly use discharge dates as new from or anniversary dates, show multiple anniversary resets for the same episode, or have claim from dates inconsistent with inpatient and SNF records. Monthly claims may be paid when the beneficiary was institutionalized for most of the month but home on the billing date. Supplier changes cluster immediately before or after discharge.
detection_signals: Count anniversary-date resets per beneficiary-HCPCS episode and flag more than one reset within 12 months.
Flag claims whose from date equals discharge date but whose delivery, possession, or home-use evidence is absent or occurs later.
Flag full-month rental claims where the beneficiary was inpatient or in an SNF for more than 80% of the month, even if home on the from date.
Flag sequential claims where the new anniversary date is not the documented discharge date after an overlapping stay.
Compare supplier-change dates with discharge dates; flag changes within plus or minus 3 days when the replacement supplier bills an initial or early-month rental modifier.
graph_signals: Supplier clusters coordinating with the same hospitals, SNFs, or discharge planners and receiving beneficiaries immediately after discharge.
Shared beneficiaries moving among suppliers at each institutional transition.
Repeated discharge-date claim patterns linked to one facility, ordering provider, or case-management vendor.
Common equipment identifiers or delivery personnel across suppliers reporting different delivery and anniversary dates.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Actual hospital or SNF stays can overlap an anniversary date and legitimately reset the billing date. Beneficiaries may change suppliers after discharge, and a home delivery or fitting process may occur immediately around discharge.
disambiguating_evidence: CWF inpatient and SNF dates, facility discharge summaries, and the supplier's annotated claim documentation.
Proof of actual home delivery, beneficiary possession, and home use on the claimed date.
Equipment serial numbers and transfer records across suppliers.
Beneficiary and facility confirmation that the item was not merely used or stored in the institution before discharge.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT beneficiary_id, hcpcs_family, COUNT(*) AS reset_count, SUM(CASE WHEN from_date = inpatient_discharge_date THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS discharge_dated_claims FROM capped_rental_claims_enriched GROUP BY beneficiary_id, hcpcs_family HAVING reset_count > 1 OR discharge_dated_claims >= 2 AND COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_npi) >= 2;

explicit: Section 110.3.2 - Date of Service for Pre-Discharge Delivery of DMEPOS
Section 210 - CWF Crossover Editing for DMEPOS Claims During an Inpatient Stay
Section 211.2.B - Policy
cms_source.inference: The discharge-date and anniversary rules are explicit. Repeated coordinated cycling and the quantitative thresholds are investigative hypotheses.

high_financial_impact.title: PEN Therapy and Pump-Reset Coordination
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Sections 30.7.1, 40.3, 50.3, and 100.2.2 establish 15-month pump rental limits, require a two-month break in medical need before another rental period, and allow special treatment when the physician changes between parenteral and enteral therapy. A coordinated supplier-clinician network may exploit therapy transitions, apparent breaks, or replacement-versus-rental pathways to extend recurring pump revenue or avoid the normal cap.

archetypes.name: Enteral/parenteral nutrition supplier
archetypes.why: The archetype directly monetizes recurring nutrients, supplies, and pump rentals; Medicare dependence 4 and compliance sophistication 2 increase exposure to documentation and continuity failures.

archetypes.name: Supplier specializing in recurring supplies or accessories
archetypes.why: Recurring revenue and volume-growth objective 4 create incentive to preserve therapy continuity and add equipment or supply claims around changes in therapy.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: Coordination 4 and access to beneficiaries 4 provide visibility into hospitalizations, therapy interruptions, and care-setting transitions that affect the two-month rule.

archetypes.name: Organized fraud-ring archetype (cooperating suppliers, clinicians, marketers, beneficiaries)
archetypes.why: Coordination 5 and willingness to exploit ambiguity 5 support synchronized prescription changes, supplier changes, and documentation of alleged breaks.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Extending pump rental payments beyond 15 months, restarting a rental episode, converting rental to a new purchase or replacement, and maintaining associated recurring supply revenue.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: PEN pump rental sequences exceed 15 months or restart shortly after the prior episode without two consecutive months of absent medically required services. Enteral-to-parenteral or parenteral-to-enteral changes occur near the rental cap and are associated with new prescriptions, supplier changes, or new pump claims. Supply claims continue during alleged breaks or appear before the revised certification date.
detection_signals: For each beneficiary-pump combination, count paid rental months across all suppliers and flag totals above 15 absent documented qualifying breaks.
Flag new pump rental periods beginning within 90 days of the prior rental end without two consecutive months showing no medically required PEN services.
Flag therapy-type changes within 60 days of month 12 or 15 of rental, especially when ordering provider, supplier, and diagnosis remain unchanged.
Flag pump purchase or replacement claims occurring near the rental cap without documented purchase date, eight-year ownership history, or revised clinical need.
Flag supply claims during purported two-month medical-need breaks or before the certification and therapy onset dates.
graph_signals: Supplier-clinician pairs repeatedly documenting enteral/parenteral switches for the same beneficiary cohort.
Beneficiaries moving between related suppliers at months 14-16 of pump rental.
Shared ordering providers, nutrition clinics, dietitians, fulfillment centers, or documentation vendors across transition claims.
Network communities with synchronized therapy changes and identical certification language.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Patients may genuinely transition between enteral and parenteral therapy, experience hospitalization or voluntary nonbilling periods, or require replacement after long-term ownership. Medical need can fluctuate in complex patients.
disambiguating_evidence: Clinical records showing the two-month absence of medically required PEN services and the reason for the therapy transition.
Physician prescriptions, revised certifications, nutrient and infusion-method changes, and therapy administration records.
Pump serial numbers, purchase invoices, rental histories, and maintenance records.
Hospital and home-health records confirming interruptions, therapy resumption, and actual pump use.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: SELECT beneficiary_id, pump_id, SUM(rental_months) AS total_rental_months, COUNT(DISTINCT supplier_npi) AS suppliers, SUM(CASE WHEN therapy_change_flag = 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS therapy_changes FROM pen_pump_episode_claims GROUP BY beneficiary_id, pump_id HAVING total_rental_months > 15 OR therapy_changes >= 1 AND MAX(rental_month_number) >= 12 AND documented_two_month_break = 0;

explicit: Section 30.7.1 - Payment for Parenteral and Enteral Pumps
Section 40.3 - Maintenance and Service of PEN Pumps
Section 50.3 - Payment for Replacement of Parenteral and Enteral Pumps
Section 100.2.2.1 - Scheduling and Documenting Certifications and Recertifications of Medical Necessity for PEN
cms_source.inference: The caps, break requirements, and therapy-change provisions are explicit. The theory of coordinated manipulation of transitions and breaks is an inference.

high_financial_impact.title: SNF and Inpatient Boundary Reclassification
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: DME is not payable for use in an SNF, while Part B prosthetics and orthotics may remain payable in institutional settings and certain noncovered Part A circumstances create different billing instructions. This creates an entity and place-of-service boundary where similar items may be routed through a supplier, SNF, hospital, or A/B MAC pathway.

archetypes.name: SNF-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: High Medicare dependence (4), institutional access (4), referral relationships (4), and coordination (4) support exposure to admission, discharge, and coverage-status boundaries.

archetypes.name: Home health-associated provider/supplier
archetypes.why: Care-setting coordination (4) and beneficiary access (4) make transitions between institutional and home settings a plausible source of billing ambiguity.

archetypes.name: Physician practice dispensing or ordering DME
archetypes.why: Access to beneficiaries and ordering providers (5 each) permits the practice to shape the item description and setting supporting medical necessity.

archetypes.name: Multi-state supplier
archetypes.why: Geographic reach (5) and moderate coding sophistication can support routing claims to different contractors or institutional billing entities.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Separate payment may be available for an item characterized as a covered P&O service or a post-discharge home-use item, while DME used in the SNF is bundled or noncovered. The financial advantage is avoiding institutional bundling and obtaining a DME fee-schedule payment.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: Supplier DME claims have dates or place-of-service indicators overlapping SNF or inpatient stays; hospital or SNF institutional claims omit corresponding P&O or DME lines; the same HCPCS family appears on supplier claims immediately before admission or immediately after discharge. Claims may alternate between 0274 P&O reporting and DME MAC professional billing.
detection_signals: Percentage of supplier claims with service dates within 0-2 days of SNF admission or discharge.
Paid supplier claims whose delivery date falls during an inpatient or SNF stay, excluding validated pre-discharge fitting rules.
Same HCPCS or clinically similar HCPCS billed by both an institution and supplier within 3 days.
Institutional episodes lacking expected bundled items despite supplier claims for the same beneficiary and diagnosis.
Frequency of supplier claims on the discharge date compared with peer distribution.
graph_signals: Repeated supplier-SNF pairs with unusually high discharge-day claim concentration.
Ordering providers affiliated with both the SNF and supplier, or shared ownership and addresses.
Beneficiary clusters linked to a particular facility's discharge planner or ordering clinician.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: P&O devices and supplies have different institutional billing rules from DME, and qualifying pre-discharge delivery may be billed with the discharge date. A beneficiary may also legitimately receive a home-use item after discharge or receive P&O outside the PPS rate.
disambiguating_evidence: Admission, discharge, and covered-status records from the SNF or hospital.
HCPCS classification showing DME versus P&O and whether the item was for home use or institutional use.
Delivery, fitting, training, and home-delivery records satisfying the two-day pre-discharge rule.
Institutional claim detail and facility responsibility documentation.

high_financial_impact.title: Installment-Purchase and Rental Classification Drift
high_financial_impact.vulnerability_hypothesis: Equipment purchased through installments reports the total equipment price on the first bill while monthly payments resemble rental amounts. Separately, claims must identify rental versus purchase and new versus used status, with distinct modifiers for BP, BR, BU, NR, NU, RR, and UE. Ambiguity between installment purchase, rental, and purchase-after-rental can produce inconsistent cumulative payment and ownership outcomes.

high_financial_impact.economic_incentive: Installment or rental coding can affect when payment is received, whether a purchase allowance is available, whether title transfers, and whether total payments exceed the applicable purchase fee schedule.
high_financial_impact.claims_manifestation: First claims reporting rental modifiers but full purchase charges; conflicting BP/BR/BU and NU/NR/UE combinations; purchase claims after rental without credit for prior rental amounts; cumulative payments exceeding the purchase fee schedule; used equipment reported as new after prior use or rental.
detection_signals: Cumulative paid amount by beneficiary-equipment episode compared with purchase fee schedule amount.
Claims with both installment indicators and ordinary rental modifiers in the same episode.
Purchase-after-rental claims lacking prior-rental offsets.
New-equipment claims where the item or serial number was previously rented, purchased, or used for another beneficiary.
Supplier-specific rates of BP, BR, BU, NR, NU, RR, and UE combinations inconsistent with peers.
graph_signals: Equipment serial numbers reused across beneficiaries or suppliers.
Supplier-finance, delivery, and billing entities sharing ownership or bank accounts.
Beneficiary transfers between related suppliers immediately before purchase conversion.
high_financial_impact.false_positive_explanation: Installment arrangements, beneficiary election changes, used demonstrator equipment, and administrative corrections can legitimately create mixed modifiers. Claims may also be submitted in separate transactions that obscure the episode chronology.
disambiguating_evidence: Contract showing whether the transaction is rental, installment purchase, or purchase after rental.
Serial-number equipment history and delivery records.
Beneficiary election documentation and title-transfer date.
Cumulative claim and adjustment history, including prior rental offsets.
high_financial_impact.detection_rule: WITH ep AS (SELECT beneficiary_id, equipment_id, SUM(allowed_amount) paid, MAX(purchase_fee_schedule) purchase_limit, MAX(CASE WHEN modifier IN ('BP','NU','NR') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) has_purchase, MAX(CASE WHEN modifier IN ('BR','BU','RR') THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) has_rental FROM dme_claims GROUP BY beneficiary_id,equipment_id) SELECT * FROM ep WHERE paid > purchase_limit * 1.05 OR (has_purchase=1 AND has_rental=1 AND paid > purchase_limit);
